children.title: Data Mining: Meaning, Definition and Concepts
children.body:
Definition of Data Mining

Data Mining is the process of discovering useful, previously unknown, valid and understandable patterns, relationships and knowledge from large volumes of data using statistical, mathematical and computational techniques.

It involves analysing large datasets to identify hidden patterns, trends, correlations and useful information that can support decision-making.

Why Do We Need Data Mining?

  • Modern organisations generate enormous amounts of data.
  • Traditional database systems are mainly designed to store, retrieve and update data, not discover hidden knowledge.
  • Manual analysis becomes difficult when datasets are large and complex.
  • Data mining helps discover patterns that are not immediately visible.
  • It supports prediction, planning, decision-making and business intelligence.

Examples

  1. Retail: Identifying products frequently purchased together to improve product placement and recommendations.
  2. Banking: Detecting suspicious transactions and identifying potential fraud.
  3. Healthcare: Analysing patient records to discover disease patterns and support diagnosis.
  4. Education: Analysing student performance to identify students who may need additional support.
  5. E-commerce: Recommending products based on browsing and purchasing history.

Characteristics of Data Mining

  • Works with large volumes of data.
  • Discovers hidden and previously unknown patterns.
  • Uses automated or semi-automated analysis techniques.
  • Combines concepts from databases, statistics, machine learning and artificial intelligence.
  • Can perform descriptive and predictive analysis.
  • Produces knowledge that can support practical decisions.

Types of Data Mining Analysis

Descriptive AnalysisPredictive Analysis
Identifies patterns and relationships present in existing data.Uses historical patterns to estimate future outcomes.
Answers: What happened? What patterns exist?Answers: What is likely to happen?
Example: Finding the most frequently purchased products.Example: Predicting future customer demand.

Data Mining vs Traditional Data Analysis

Traditional Data AnalysisData Mining
Usually investigates specific questions.Discovers hidden patterns and relationships.
Often relies on predefined queries.Uses algorithms to identify patterns.
Can work with relatively small datasets.Often designed for large and complex datasets.
Example: Finding total sales in a month.Example: Discovering customer purchasing behaviour.

Revision Points

  • Data mining is also called Knowledge Discovery from Data in a broader context.
  • Data mining is one important step in the KDD process.
  • The main objective is to extract useful knowledge from data.
  • Applications include banking, healthcare, retail, education and scientific research.

children.title: Applications of Data Mining
children.body:
Major Applications

1. Retail and Marketing

  • Market basket analysis.
  • Customer segmentation.
  • Product recommendation.
  • Sales forecasting.
  • Customer purchasing behaviour analysis.

Example: A supermarket discovers that customers who purchase bread frequently purchase butter. It can use this information for product placement and promotions.

2. Banking and Finance

  • Credit risk assessment.
  • Fraud detection.
  • Customer classification.
  • Loan approval analysis.
  • Stock market trend analysis.

Example: A bank analyses transaction patterns to identify unusual transactions that may indicate fraud.

3. Healthcare and Medicine

  • Disease prediction.
  • Patient classification.
  • Medical image analysis.
  • Treatment effectiveness analysis.
  • Identifying disease risk factors.

4. Education

  • Student performance prediction.
  • Dropout prediction.
  • Learning behaviour analysis.
  • Course recommendation.

5. Telecommunications

  • Customer churn prediction.
  • Network fault detection.
  • Usage pattern analysis.
  • Fraudulent usage identification.

6. E-commerce

  • Personalised recommendations.
  • Customer behaviour analysis.
  • Shopping trend prediction.
  • Review and sentiment analysis.

Advantages of Data Mining

  • Helps discover hidden patterns in large datasets.
  • Improves decision-making.
  • Supports forecasting and prediction.
  • Identifies fraud and unusual behaviour.
  • Improves customer understanding.
  • Helps optimise organisational operations.

Limitations and Challenges

  • Data quality: Incomplete, incorrect or inconsistent data can produce misleading results.
  • Privacy: Personal information must be protected.
  • Security: Sensitive datasets require appropriate access control.
  • Scalability: Processing very large datasets can require significant resources.
  • Interpretability: Some complex models are difficult to understand.
  • Bias: Biased training data can produce unfair predictions.

Exam Tip

For an application-based question, explain the domain, the data being analysed, the mining technique and the benefit obtained. Do not simply list the application names.

children.title: Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD)
children.body:
Definition

Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) is the overall process of identifying valid, novel, useful and understandable patterns from large datasets.

KDD is a complete knowledge extraction process that involves multiple stages, starting with raw data and ending with useful knowledge.

Stages of the KDD Process

  1. Data Cleaning: Removes noise and handles missing or inconsistent values.
  2. Data Integration: Combines data from multiple sources into a unified dataset.
  3. Data Selection: Selects relevant data required for analysis.
  4. Data Transformation: Converts data into a suitable format for mining.
  5. Data Mining: Applies algorithms to discover patterns and relationships.
  6. Pattern Evaluation: Identifies interesting, useful and valid patterns.
  7. Knowledge Presentation: Presents discovered knowledge using reports, visualisations and other understandable representations.

KDD Process Flow

Raw Data

   v
Data Cleaning
   |
   v
Data Integration
   |
   v
Data Selection
   |
   v
Data Transformation

   v
Data Mining
   |
   v
Pattern Evaluation
   |
   v
Knowledge Presentation
   |
   v
Useful Knowledge

Explanation of Each Stage

1. Data Cleaning

Real-world data may contain missing values, duplicate records, noise and incorrect entries. Cleaning improves data quality before analysis.

Example: Replacing or appropriately handling a missing customer age value.

2. Data Integration

Data from different databases or sources are combined into a common dataset.

Example: Combining customer information from sales, billing and support databases.

3. Data Selection

Only the records and attributes relevant to the mining task are selected.

Example: Selecting customer age, purchase history and income for customer segmentation.

4. Data Transformation

Data are converted into an appropriate form for mining algorithms.

Example: Normalising numerical values or converting categorical attributes into numerical representations.

5. Data Mining

Algorithms are applied to discover patterns, relationships, clusters or predictive models.

Example: Applying a classification algorithm to predict whether a customer will leave a service.

6. Pattern Evaluation

Discovered patterns are evaluated to determine their validity, usefulness and interestingness.

Example: Checking whether a discovered purchasing relationship is sufficiently frequent and reliable.

7. Knowledge Presentation

Useful patterns are presented in a form that users can understand, such as graphs, reports, tables and visualisations.

Important Properties of Discovered Knowledge

  • Valid: The pattern should be reliable and applicable to the data.
  • Novel: The pattern should reveal something previously unknown or not obvious.
  • Useful: It should provide practical value.
  • Understandable: It should be interpretable by users.

Important Point

Data mining is only one stage of the complete KDD process. KDD includes preprocessing, mining, evaluation and presentation.

children.title: Difference Between KDD and Data Mining
children.body:
Basic Difference

KDD refers to the complete process of extracting useful knowledge from data, whereas data mining refers specifically to the algorithmic step in which patterns are discovered.

KDDData Mining
Complete knowledge discovery process.One stage of the KDD process.
Includes cleaning, integration, selection, transformation, mining, evaluation and presentation.Focuses on applying algorithms to discover patterns.
Begins with raw data and produces useful knowledge.Works on prepared data to generate patterns or models.
Includes human judgement and domain knowledge throughout the process.Primarily involves computational and analytical techniques.
Has a broader scope.Has a narrower scope.

Example

Consider a supermarket that wants to understand customer purchasing behaviour.

  1. KDD: The supermarket collects sales data, cleans missing records, integrates multiple store databases, selects relevant transactions, transforms the data, applies mining algorithms, evaluates patterns and presents useful findings.
  2. Data Mining: The supermarket applies an association rule mining algorithm to discover that customers who buy bread frequently buy butter.

Relationship

KDD = Data Preparation
    + Data Mining
    + Pattern Evaluation
    + Knowledge Presentation

The expression above is a conceptual summary, not a mathematical equation.

Common Exam Question

Question: Explain the KDD process and distinguish between KDD and data mining.

Answer structure: Start with the definition of KDD, draw the seven-stage flow diagram, explain each stage briefly and conclude with a comparison table showing that data mining is a subset of KDD.

children.title: 3. Architecture of a Typical Data Mining System
Data Mining System Architecture
children.body:
Introduction

A data mining system architecture describes the major components involved in collecting data, preparing it, discovering patterns and presenting the resulting knowledge to users.

Main Components

  1. Database, Data Warehouse or Other Information Repository: Stores the data that will be mined. Data may come from relational databases, data warehouses, files or other information sources.
  2. Database or Data Warehouse Server: Retrieves relevant data and provides access to the information repository. It may perform database queries and data management operations.
  3. Knowledge Base: Contains domain knowledge that can guide the mining process and help evaluate discovered patterns.
  4. Data Mining Engine: The core component that performs mining tasks using algorithms such as classification, clustering, association analysis and prediction.
  5. Pattern Evaluation Module: Evaluates discovered patterns and identifies those that satisfy interestingness criteria.
  6. Graphical User Interface: Allows users to interact with the system, specify mining tasks and view results.

Architecture Diagram

       User
        |
        v
  Graphical User Interface
        |
        v
  Pattern Evaluation Module
        |
        v
     Data Mining Engine
        |           ^
        |           |
        v       Knowledge Base
 Database / Data Warehouse
        |
        v
   Data Repository

Note: This is a simplified conceptual representation. In a complete architecture, the user interface, mining engine, pattern evaluation module and knowledge base interact with each other, and the database server manages access to the data repository.

Functions of Each Component

1. Data Repository

Stores the original data. It may contain structured, semi-structured or unstructured information.

2. Database or Data Warehouse Server

Handles data retrieval and communication with the repository. It provides the mining system with the required data.

3. Knowledge Base

Stores useful domain information, concept hierarchies, constraints and metadata that can guide the mining process.

4. Data Mining Engine

Performs the actual mining operations. It may include algorithms for:

  • Association rule mining.
  • Classification.
  • Prediction.
  • Clustering.
  • Outlier analysis.
  • Evolution and trend analysis.

5. Pattern Evaluation Module

Filters and evaluates discovered patterns using measures such as support, confidence, accuracy or other task-specific criteria.

6. Graphical User Interface

Allows users to define mining queries, specify constraints, select algorithms and inspect results.

Working of a Data Mining System

  1. The user specifies a mining task through the graphical interface.
  2. The system accesses relevant data from the database or data warehouse.
  3. The data mining engine applies the selected algorithms.
  4. The knowledge base provides relevant domain information or constraints.
  5. The pattern evaluation module identifies useful patterns.
  6. The results are presented to the user through the interface.

Revision Points

  • The data mining engine is the core processing component.
  • The knowledge base guides the mining process.
  • The pattern evaluation module identifies interesting patterns.
  • The graphical user interface enables user interaction.
  • The database server manages access to stored data.

children.title: Data Mining Functionalities
children.body:
Introduction

Data mining functionalities describe the different kinds of knowledge and patterns that can be discovered from a dataset. They determine what type of analysis a data mining system can perform.

1. Concept or Class Description

Describes the general characteristics of data belonging to a particular class. It includes two important activities.

Data Characterisation

Summarises the general features of a target class of data.

Example: Summarising the characteristics of customers who purchase premium products.

Data Discrimination

Compares the characteristics of one target class with those of one or more contrasting classes.

Example: Comparing customers who purchase premium products with customers who purchase basic products.

2. Frequent Pattern, Association and Correlation Analysis

Discovers frequently occurring patterns, relationships and correlations among items or attributes in a dataset.

Example: Customers who purchase milk frequently purchase bread.

An association rule is represented as:

$$X \Rightarrow Y$$

Here, X is the antecedent and Y is the consequent.

3. Classification

Classification is a supervised learning technique that learns from labelled training data and assigns new records to predefined classes.

Example: Classifying an email as spam or not spam.

4. Prediction

Prediction estimates unknown or future numerical values based on existing data.

Example: Predicting the sales revenue of a business next month.

5. Clustering

Clustering groups similar data objects together without predefined class labels.

Example: Dividing customers into groups based on purchasing behaviour.

6. Outlier Analysis

Identifies data objects that differ significantly from the general behaviour of a dataset.

Example: Detecting an unusually large banking transaction that may indicate fraud.

7. Evolution and Trend Analysis

Studies changes, trends and patterns over time.

Example: Analysing monthly sales to identify seasonal purchasing trends.

Comparison of Major Functionalities

FunctionalityPurposeExample
CharacterisationSummarises a target class.Profile of premium customers.
DiscriminationCompares different classes.Premium vs basic customers.
AssociationFinds relationships between items.Bread and butter purchases.
ClassificationAssigns predefined class labels.Spam detection.
PredictionEstimates numerical or future values.Sales forecasting.
ClusteringGroups similar objects.Customer segmentation.
Outlier AnalysisFinds unusual objects.Fraud detection.
Evolution AnalysisStudies changes over time.Seasonal sales trends.

Important Distinction

  • Classification: Uses predefined classes and labelled training data.
  • Clustering: Discovers groups without predefined labels.
  • Prediction: Estimates an unknown or future value.
  • Association: Discovers relationships between items or attributes.

children.title: Data Warehouse: Definition and Characteristics
children.body:
Definition

A Data Warehouse is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile collection of data designed to support management decision-making.

This definition is commonly associated with William H. Inmon, who is widely regarded as a pioneer of data warehousing.

Four Characteristics of a Data Warehouse

1. Subject-Oriented

Data are organised around important subjects of an organisation rather than individual operational processes.

Example: A sales data warehouse organises information about customers, products, sales and revenue.

2. Integrated

Data are collected from different sources and converted into a consistent format.

Example: Different departments may store dates as DD-MM-YYYY and MM-DD-YYYY. Integration converts them into a common format.

3. Time-Variant

A data warehouse stores historical data over a long period. Each record is associated with a time dimension or historical context.

Example: A company stores sales information for the last ten years to analyse yearly trends.

4. Non-Volatile

Once data are loaded into the warehouse, they are generally not frequently modified or deleted like operational transaction records. Data are primarily loaded and queried.

Example: Historical sales records are retained for long-term analysis.

Operational Database vs Data Warehouse

Operational Database (OLTP)Data Warehouse (OLAP)
Designed for daily business transactions.Designed for analysis and decision-making.
Stores current operational data.Stores historical and integrated data.
Frequently updated through insert, update and delete operations.Primarily loaded and queried.
Usually organised around individual applications and transactions.Usually organised around analytical subjects.
Supports short and simple transactions.Supports complex analytical queries.
Examples: Banking transactions and order processing.Examples: Sales trend and business performance analysis.

Advantages of Data Warehousing

  • Provides a centralised view of organisational data.
  • Supports historical analysis.
  • Improves reporting and decision-making.
  • Combines data from multiple sources.
  • Supports complex analytical queries.
  • Reduces the need to run heavy analytical queries on operational systems.

Data Warehouse vs Database

A database is a general-purpose organised collection of data. A data warehouse is specifically designed to integrate historical data and support analytical processing. A data warehouse may itself use database technology.

Exam Revision

For the question Define a Data Warehouse and explain its characteristics, write the definition first and explain all four characteristics using the keywords subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile. Include one example for each.

children.title: Data Warehouse Architecture
children.body:
Introduction

Data warehouse architecture describes how data are collected from different sources, transformed, stored and made available for analytical processing and decision-making.

Three-Tier Data Warehouse Architecture

A commonly used data warehouse architecture consists of three tiers.

1. Bottom Tier: Data Warehouse Server

The bottom tier contains the data warehouse database and data integration processes.

  • Data are collected from operational databases, external sources and files.
  • ETL processes extract, transform and load the data.
  • The processed data are stored in the data warehouse.
  • Data marts may be created for individual departments.

2. Middle Tier: OLAP Server

The middle tier contains the OLAP server, which provides multidimensional analytical processing.

  • Supports multidimensional views of data.
  • Processes analytical queries.
  • Provides operations such as roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice and pivot.

3. Top Tier: Front-End Tools

The top tier contains user-facing tools for accessing and analysing warehouse data.

  • Query tools.
  • Reporting tools.
  • Data analysis tools.
  • Data mining tools.
  • Visualisation and dashboard tools.

ETL Process

ETL stands for Extract, Transform and Load. It is a data integration process commonly used to populate a data warehouse.

1. Extract

Collects data from different source systems such as databases, files and external systems.

2. Transform

Converts data into a consistent and suitable format. It may involve cleaning, validation, standardisation, deduplication and integration.

3. Load

Stores the transformed data in the target data warehouse.

Types of OLAP Servers

  • ROLAP: Relational OLAP stores multidimensional data in relational tables and performs analytical queries using relational database technology.
  • MOLAP: Multidimensional OLAP stores data in multidimensional structures or cubes for efficient analytical access.
  • HOLAP: Hybrid OLAP combines relational and multidimensional storage approaches.

Advantages of Three-Tier Architecture

  • Separates data storage, analytical processing and presentation.
  • Supports large-scale analytical workloads.
  • Improves organisation and maintainability.
  • Allows multiple analytical tools to access warehouse data.
  • Supports different OLAP implementation approaches.

Exam Tip

Draw the three tiers from bottom to top. Clearly label the data sources, ETL process, data warehouse, OLAP server and front-end tools. Explain each tier separately.

children.title: Multidimensional Data Model: Concepts and Components
children.body:
Definition

The Multidimensional Data Model represents data in multiple dimensions, allowing users to analyse information from different perspectives.

It is widely used in data warehouses and OLAP systems because it makes complex analytical queries easier to understand and perform.

Main Components

1. Fact Table

A fact table stores quantitative measurements of a business process along with foreign keys referencing related dimension tables.

Example: A sales fact table may contain product ID, customer ID, time ID, store ID, quantity sold and total sales amount.

Common measures include:

  • Total sales.
  • Quantity sold.
  • Profit.
  • Discount amount.

2. Dimension Table

A dimension table stores descriptive information used to analyse facts.

Example: A product dimension may contain product ID, product name, brand, category and price.

3. Measures

Measures are numerical values stored in or derived from the fact table. They are analysed across different dimensions.

Examples: Revenue, quantity, cost and profit.

4. Dimensions

Dimensions represent the perspectives through which data are analysed.

Examples: Time, product, customer and location.

Example: Sales Data Cube

Consider a retail company that wants to analyse sales based on three dimensions: Time, Product and Location.

  • Time: Day, month, quarter and year.
  • Product: Product name, category and brand.
  • Location: City, state and country.
  • Measure: Total sales revenue.
                 TIME
                   |
                   |
                   +--------- PRODUCT
                  /
                 /
             LOCATION

        Measure: Sales Revenue

A cube allows the company to ask questions such as total sales of laptops in Kerala during 2025.

Types of Measures

1. Distributive Measures

A measure is distributive if the result can be computed by dividing the data into subsets, calculating the measure for each subset and combining the results.

Examples: SUM, COUNT, MIN and MAX.

2. Algebraic Measures

A measure is algebraic if it can be computed using a fixed number of distributive measures.

Examples: Average and standard deviation.

Average is calculated using:

$$\text{Average}=\frac{\text{SUM}}{\text{COUNT}}$$

3. Holistic Measures

A measure is holistic if there is no fixed-size summary that is sufficient to calculate the exact result for arbitrary partitions.

Example: Median and mode in the general case.

OLAP Cube Example

Suppose the following sales records are stored:

YearProductCitySales
2024LaptopKochi50000
2024PhoneKochi30000
2025LaptopTrivandrum60000
2025PhoneKochi35000

Using these dimensions, the company can calculate sales by year, product or city, and combine these perspectives to analyse more detailed patterns.

Advantages

  • Provides multiple perspectives of data.
  • Simplifies complex analytical queries.
  • Supports aggregation and summarisation.
  • Allows users to explore data at different levels of detail.
  • Supports decision-making and business analysis.

Fact Table vs Dimension Table

Fact TableDimension Table
Contains measurable business events.Contains descriptive information.
Usually contains foreign keys.Usually contains primary keys.
Stores quantitative measures.Stores descriptive attributes.
Usually contains a large number of rows.Usually contains fewer rows than the fact table.
Example: Sales_Fact.Example: Product_Dimension.

Types of Fact Table Measures

  • Additive: Can be summed across all dimensions. Example: Sales amount.
  • Semi-additive: Can be summed across some dimensions but not all. Example: Account balance across accounts but generally not across time.
  • Non-additive: Cannot be meaningfully summed across dimensions. Example: Ratios and percentages.

Granularity

Granularity refers to the level of detail represented by each row in a fact table.

Example: A sales fact table may store one row per individual transaction or one row per product per store per day. Transaction-level data has finer granularity.

Revision Points

  • Fact tables contain measures and foreign keys.
  • Dimension tables contain descriptive attributes.
  • Granularity determines the level of detail in the fact table.
  • Always identify the grain of a fact table before designing it.

children.title: Star Schema
children.body:
Definition

A Star Schema is a data warehouse schema in which a central fact table is directly connected to multiple dimension tables. Its structure resembles a star.

Structure

The central fact table stores measures and foreign keys. Each surrounding dimension table stores descriptive attributes.

              Time_Dim
                 |
                 |
Product_Dim -- Sales_Fact -- Customer_Dim
                 |
                 |
              Store_Dim

Example

Consider a sales data warehouse.

Sales_Fact: Time_ID, Product_ID, Customer_ID, Store_ID, Quantity, Sales_Amount.

Time_Dim: Time_ID, Date, Month, Quarter, Year.

Product_Dim: Product_ID, Product_Name, Category, Brand.

Customer_Dim: Customer_ID, Customer_Name, Gender, City.

Store_Dim: Store_ID, Store_Name, City, State.

Characteristics

  • Contains one central fact table.
  • Dimension tables connect directly to the fact table.
  • Dimension tables are generally denormalised.
  • Queries are relatively simple because fewer joins are needed.
  • Commonly used in data marts and analytical systems.

Advantages

  • Simple to understand and design.
  • Easy for users to navigate.
  • Provides good query performance for many analytical workloads.
  • Requires fewer joins than a snowflake schema for equivalent dimension structures.

Disadvantages

  • May introduce data redundancy in dimension tables.
  • Can require more storage.
  • Dimension updates may require changes in multiple repeated records.

Exam Tip

Draw a central fact table and connect it directly to at least four dimension tables. Label the measures and dimension attributes in the explanation.

children.title: Snowflake Schema
children.body:
Definition

A Snowflake Schema is a data warehouse schema in which dimension tables are normalised into multiple related tables. Its structure resembles a snowflake.

Structure

The fact table connects to dimension tables, and some dimensions are further divided into related sub-dimension tables.

                  Year_Dim
                     |
                 Time_Dim
                     |
                     |
Product_Dim -- Sales_Fact -- Customer_Dim
    |                            |
Category_Dim                  City_Dim
                                 |
                              State_Dim

Example

In a product dimension, product details and category details can be stored separately.

  • Product_Dim: Product_ID, Product_Name, Category_ID.
  • Category_Dim: Category_ID, Category_Name.

Similarly, a location dimension may be divided into city, state and country tables.

Characteristics

  • Dimension tables are normalised.
  • Contains additional relationships among dimension tables.
  • Reduces repeated descriptive data.
  • Requires more joins for many analytical queries.

Advantages

  • Reduces redundancy.
  • Can improve consistency of dimension data.
  • May reduce storage requirements for repeated attributes.
  • Supports complex hierarchical dimensions.

Disadvantages

  • More complex schema design.
  • Queries may require additional joins.
  • Can be harder for end users to understand.
  • Query performance may be lower for some workloads because of additional joins.

children.title: Fact Constellation Schema and Schema Comparison
children.body:
Definition

A Fact Constellation Schema, also called a galaxy schema, contains multiple fact tables that share one or more dimension tables.

Structure

For example, a retail organisation may maintain separate Sales_Fact and Shipping_Fact tables that share Time_Dim, Product_Dim and Store_Dim.

             Time_Dim

             /      \
      Sales_Fact   Shipping_Fact
          |  \       /   |
          |   \     /    |
     Product_Dim   Store_Dim

Characteristics

  • Contains multiple fact tables.
  • Fact tables can share common dimensions.
  • Supports multiple business processes.
  • Suitable for large and complex data warehouse systems.

FeatureStarSnowflakeFact Constellation
Fact tablesUsually oneUsually oneMultiple
Dimension structureDenormalisedNormalisedMay be normalised or denormalised
ComplexityLowMedium to highHigh
JoinsFewerMoreDepends on design
RedundancyGenerally higherGenerally lowerDepends on dimensions

How to Identify Each Schema

  • Star: One central fact table with direct links to dimension tables.
  • Snowflake: Dimension tables are split into related normalised tables.
  • Fact Constellation: Multiple fact tables share dimensions.

Exam Tip

Practise drawing all three schemas. In comparison questions, explain the number of fact tables, dimension normalisation, complexity and join requirements.

children.title: OLAP: Definition and Concepts
children.body:
Definition

Online Analytical Processing (OLAP) is a technology used to perform multidimensional analysis of data stored in a data warehouse. It enables users to analyse data from different perspectives and perform complex analytical queries.

Purpose of OLAP

  • Analyse large volumes of historical data.
  • Support management decision-making.
  • Identify trends and patterns.
  • Summarise data at different levels of detail.
  • Compare performance across products, locations and time periods.

OLAP Cube

An OLAP cube is a multidimensional representation of data. Its dimensions provide different perspectives, while its measures represent numerical values to be analysed.

For example, a sales cube may contain:

  • Time dimension.
  • Product dimension.
  • Location dimension.
  • Measure: Sales amount.

Example

A company wants to analyse total sales based on year, product and location. OLAP allows the company to view total sales by year, compare products across cities and examine sales for a particular year and product category.

OLAP Characteristics

  • Multidimensional data representation.
  • Fast analytical query processing.
  • Historical data analysis.
  • Aggregation and summarisation.
  • Interactive exploration of data.
  • Supports complex business analysis.

OLAP vs OLTP

OLAPOLTP
Online Analytical Processing.Online Transaction Processing.
Designed for analysis.Designed for transactions.
Uses historical and integrated data.Primarily uses current operational data.
Complex analytical queries.Short and frequent transactions.
Generally read-intensive.Supports frequent inserts, updates and deletes.
Used by analysts and management.Used by operational applications and staff.
Example: Annual sales analysis.Example: Processing a customer payment.

Types of OLAP Systems

1. MOLAP

Multidimensional OLAP stores data in multidimensional structures or cubes. It can provide fast access to precomputed aggregates.

2. ROLAP

Relational OLAP stores data in relational database tables and performs analytical operations using SQL and relational database technology.

3. HOLAP

Hybrid OLAP combines relational and multidimensional approaches. Detailed data may remain in relational tables, while summaries may be stored in multidimensional structures.

Comparison of OLAP Types

FeatureMOLAPROLAPHOLAP
StorageMultidimensional structuresRelational tablesCombination
Query performanceOften fast for supported cube queriesDepends on relational query optimisationCombines both approaches
ScalabilityDepends on cube size and implementationUses relational database scalabilityBalances both approaches
Storage requirementMay require additional cube storageUses relational storageDepends on implementation

Revision Points

  • OLAP is used for multidimensional analysis.
  • OLTP is used for transaction processing.
  • MOLAP uses multidimensional storage.
  • ROLAP uses relational storage.
  • HOLAP combines both approaches.

children.title: OLAP Operations: Roll-Up, Drill-Down, Slice, Dice and Pivot
children.body:
Introduction

OLAP operations allow users to interactively explore multidimensional data by changing the level of detail, selecting dimensions and viewing data from different perspectives.

1. Roll-Up

Definition: Roll-up is an operation that summarises data by moving from a lower level of detail to a higher level in a dimension hierarchy or by reducing dimensions.

Example: Summarising daily sales into monthly sales and monthly sales into yearly sales.

Day -> Month -> Quarter -> Year

Detailed Data -> Summarised Data

Result: Less detailed and more aggregated data.

2. Drill-Down

Definition: Drill-down is the opposite of roll-up. It moves from summarised data to more detailed data.

Example: Moving from yearly sales to quarterly sales, then monthly sales and daily sales.

Year -> Quarter -> Month -> Day

Summarised Data -> Detailed Data

Result: More detailed information.

3. Slice

Definition: Slice selects a single fixed value for one dimension of a multidimensional cube, producing a smaller view of the data.

Example: Selecting only the year 2025 from a sales cube containing multiple years, while analysing product and location dimensions.

Result: A lower-dimensional view of the cube.

4. Dice

Definition: Dice selects a range or set of values across two or more dimensions to create a smaller subcube.

Example: Selecting sales for years 2024 and 2025, products Laptop and Phone, and locations Kochi and Trivandrum.

Result: A subcube containing only the selected combinations.

5. Pivot (Rotate)

Definition: Pivot changes the orientation of the multidimensional data view to present information from a different perspective.

Example: Changing a report that displays products as rows and years as columns into one that displays years as rows and products as columns.

Result: A rearranged presentation of the same underlying data.

OLAP Operations Summary

OperationMeaningExample
Roll-UpSummarises data.Day to month.
Drill-DownShows more detail.Year to quarter.
SliceFixes one dimension to a single value.Sales for 2025 only.
DiceSelects values across multiple dimensions.Selected years, products and cities.
PivotChanges the orientation of the data view.Swap rows and columns.

Combined Example

Consider a sales cube with Time, Product and Location dimensions.

  1. Roll-Up: Aggregate monthly sales into yearly sales.
  2. Drill-Down: Examine the monthly sales within a selected year.
  3. Slice: Select sales for the year 2025.
  4. Dice: Select Laptop and Phone sales in Kochi and Trivandrum during 2024 and 2025.
  5. Pivot: Change the report layout to display locations as rows and products as columns.

How to Differentiate Slice and Dice

SliceDice
Selects one fixed value of a dimension.Selects a set or range of values across multiple dimensions.
Produces a simpler lower-dimensional view.Produces a smaller subcube.
Example: Year = 2025.Example: Year in 2024 and 2025, Product in Laptop and Phone.

How to Differentiate Roll-Up and Drill-Down

Roll-UpDrill-Down
Moves towards summarisation.Moves towards detail.
Reduces the level of detail.Increases the level of detail.
Day to month.Year to month.

Exam Tip

OLAP operations are important for diagram-based and comparison questions. Memorise the direction of roll-up and drill-down, and use clear examples to distinguish slice from dice.

children.title: Data Preprocessing: Meaning, Need and Importance
children.body:
Definition

Data preprocessing is the process of converting raw, incomplete, inconsistent and noisy data into a clean and suitable format for data mining and analysis.

Real-world data is rarely perfect. It may contain missing values, duplicate records, incorrect entries, inconsistent formats and irrelevant attributes. Data preprocessing improves data quality before applying mining algorithms.

Why Is Data Preprocessing Required?

  • Incomplete data: Some records may have missing attribute values.
  • Noisy data: Data may contain random errors or incorrect values.
  • Inconsistent data: Different sources may use different formats or representations.
  • Duplicate data: The same record may appear multiple times.
  • Irrelevant data: Some attributes may not contribute to the mining task.
  • Large data volume: Data may need to be reduced to make processing efficient.

Major Data Preprocessing Tasks

  1. Data Cleaning: Handles missing values, noise and inconsistencies.
  2. Data Integration: Combines data from multiple sources.
  3. Data Transformation: Converts data into an appropriate format.
  4. Data Reduction: Reduces data size while preserving important information.
  5. Data Discretization: Converts continuous numerical values into intervals or categories.
  6. Concept Hierarchy Generation: Organises detailed values into higher-level concepts.

children.title: Data Cleaning and Handling Missing Values
children.body:
Definition of Data Cleaning

Data cleaning is the process of detecting and correcting or removing inaccurate, incomplete, inconsistent and noisy data from a dataset.

It improves the reliability and quality of data before data mining.

Common Data Cleaning Problems

  • Missing attribute values.
  • Noisy data.
  • Incorrect data values.
  • Duplicate records.
  • Inconsistent data formats.
  • Conflicting values from different sources.

Handling Missing Values

A missing value occurs when an attribute value is not available for a particular record.

Example:

StudentAgeMarks
A2085
BNULL90
C2175

The age attribute of student B is missing.

Methods for Handling Missing Values

1. Ignore the Tuple

Remove the entire record containing the missing value.

Example: Delete student B's record if the missing value makes the record unusable and enough other records are available.

Advantage: Simple to implement.

Disadvantage: Can result in loss of useful information, especially when many records contain missing values.

2. Fill in the Missing Value Manually

A person uses domain knowledge or another reliable source to enter the missing value.

Example: Checking the student's original registration form to find the missing age.

Advantage: Can provide accurate values when reliable information exists.

Disadvantage: Time-consuming and difficult for large datasets.

3. Use a Global Constant

Replace missing values with a predefined constant such as Unknown, NA or -1, provided that the replacement is suitable for the attribute.

Example: Replace a missing city with Unknown.

Advantage: Simple and preserves the record.

Disadvantage: The artificial value may affect statistical analysis or algorithms if it is treated as a genuine value.

4. Use the Attribute Mean

For numerical data, replace a missing value with the mean of the available values for that attribute.

Formula:

$$\bar{x}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i}{n}$$

Example: Available ages are 20, 22, 24 and 26.

$$\text{Mean}=\frac{20+22+24+26}{4}=23$$

A missing age can be replaced with 23.

Limitation: The mean is sensitive to extreme values.

5. Use the Class-Specific Mean

Replace the missing value using the mean calculated from records belonging to the same class.

Example: If a missing salary belongs to an employee classified as a manager, use the average salary of other managers rather than the overall employee average.

This can provide a more representative estimate when different classes have different distributions.

6. Use the Most Probable Value

Estimate the missing value using statistical methods or machine learning techniques such as regression, decision trees or Bayesian methods.

Example: Predict a missing salary using education, experience and job role.

Advantage: Can use relationships among multiple attributes.

Disadvantage: More complex and dependent on the quality of the prediction model.

Comparison of Missing Value Methods

MethodApproachLimitation
Ignore tupleDelete incomplete record.Loss of information.
Manual fillingUse external or domain knowledge.Time-consuming.
Global constantUse a fixed replacement.May distort analysis.
Attribute meanUse overall numerical mean.Sensitive to outliers.
Class-specific meanUse mean within a class.Requires suitable class information.
Most probable valueUse a prediction model.Requires model building and validation.

Missing Data Mechanisms

In statistical analysis, missing values are often classified according to why they are missing.

  • MCAR (Missing Completely At Random): The probability of a value being missing is unrelated to observed or unobserved data.
  • MAR (Missing At Random): Missingness depends on observed variables but not on the missing value itself after accounting for observed data.
  • MNAR (Missing Not At Random): Missingness depends on the missing value itself or other unobserved information.

Important Exam Points

  • Mean replacement is suitable for numerical attributes but can be affected by outliers.
  • Mode replacement is commonly used for categorical attributes.
  • Deleting records is not always appropriate when many values are missing.
  • Choose an imputation technique based on the attribute type, missingness mechanism and analysis objective.

children.title: Noisy Data and Noise Handling Techniques
children.body:
Definition of Noisy Data

Noisy data is data containing random errors, incorrect values or unwanted variations that do not accurately represent the underlying information.

Noise can occur because of faulty sensors, human data entry errors, measurement problems or data transmission errors.

Example

Consider the following salary values in a dataset:

25000, 26000, 27000, 25500, 2500000

The value 2500000 may be an erroneous entry or an unusual but genuine observation. It must be investigated before correction or removal.

Types of Noise

  • Random noise: Unpredictable variations in measured values.
  • Measurement error: Incorrect values produced by measurement devices.
  • Human error: Mistakes during manual data entry.
  • Transmission error: Data corruption during communication.

Techniques for Handling Noisy Data

1. Binning

Binning is a smoothing technique that sorts data and divides it into groups called bins. Values inside each bin are smoothed using statistical measures.

Consider the sorted values:

4, 8, 9, 15, 21, 24, 25, 28, 34

Divide them into three equal-depth bins:

  • Bin 1: 4, 8, 9
  • Bin 2: 15, 21, 24
  • Bin 3: 25, 28, 34

Smoothing by bin means: Replace every value in a bin with the mean of that bin.

  • Bin 1 mean = (4 + 8 + 9) / 3 = 7.
  • Bin 2 mean = (15 + 21 + 24) / 3 = 20.
  • Bin 3 mean = (25 + 28 + 34) / 3 = 29.

Smoothed data: 7, 7, 7, 20, 20, 20, 29, 29, 29.

Smoothing by bin medians: Replace every value with the median of its bin.

  • Bin 1 median = 8.
  • Bin 2 median = 21.
  • Bin 3 median = 28.

Smoothed data: 8, 8, 8, 21, 21, 21, 28, 28, 28.

Smoothing by bin boundaries: Replace each value with the nearest boundary value of its bin, usually the minimum or maximum.

For Bin 1 with boundaries 4 and 9, the values 4, 8 and 9 become 4, 9 and 9 respectively.

2. Regression

Regression fits a mathematical function to the data. Values that deviate significantly from the fitted trend can be investigated as possible noise.

Example: A regression line models the relationship between advertising expenditure and sales. Observations far from the line may require investigation.

3. Clustering

Clustering groups similar data objects. Objects that do not belong to any major cluster or lie far from their cluster may be potential outliers.

Example: In customer spending data, a record with unusually different spending behaviour may be identified for investigation.

4. Outlier Analysis

Outlier detection identifies records that differ significantly from the general distribution of the data.

Common approaches include statistical methods, distance-based methods and density-based methods.

5. Manual Inspection

Domain experts inspect suspicious records and determine whether they represent errors or genuine unusual events.

Comparison of Noise Handling Methods

MethodBasic Idea
BinningSmooths values using bin means, medians or boundaries.
RegressionFits a model and investigates deviations.
ClusteringIdentifies objects that do not fit major groups.
Outlier analysisDetects unusually different observations.
Manual inspectionUses domain knowledge to verify suspicious records.

Important Distinction: Noise vs Outlier

Noise refers to unwanted errors or random variation. An outlier is an observation that differs significantly from other observations. An outlier may be a genuine and important observation rather than an error.

Exam Tip

For a binning question, show the sorted data, bin formation, calculation of means or medians and final smoothed values. Do not remove unusual values automatically without checking whether they are genuine.

children.title: Data Integration: Meaning, Need and Issues
children.body:
Definition

Data integration is the process of combining data from multiple heterogeneous sources into a unified and consistent dataset.

Organisations often store information in different databases, files and applications. Data integration brings these sources together for comprehensive analysis.

Example

A retail company has three separate systems:

  • Customer database containing customer details.
  • Sales database containing purchase transactions.
  • Inventory database containing product stock details.

Data integration combines relevant information from these systems to analyse customer purchases and product availability.

Need for Data Integration

  • Combines data distributed across multiple sources.
  • Provides a unified view of organisational information.
  • Reduces inconsistencies among systems.
  • Supports data warehousing.
  • Enables comprehensive data mining and analysis.

Major Issues in Data Integration

1. Schema Integration

Different data sources may use different structures and attribute names for the same concept.

Example: One database uses Customer_ID, while another uses Cust_No for the same identifier.

The schemas must be mapped into a common structure.

2. Entity Identification Problem

The same real-world entity may be represented differently in multiple datasets.

Example: The customer name Arun Kumar in one database and A. Kumar in another may refer to the same person.

Entity resolution determines whether these records represent the same entity.

3. Redundancy

Some attributes may be duplicated or derivable from other attributes.

Example: A dataset stores both Date_of_Birth and Age. Age can be calculated from Date_of_Birth and the reference date.

Redundant attributes may be identified using correlation analysis and domain knowledge.

4. Data Value Conflicts

Different sources may use different representations, units or values for the same information.

Examples:

  • Height stored in centimetres in one system and metres in another.
  • Date represented as DD-MM-YYYY in one source and MM-DD-YYYY in another.
  • Gender represented as M/F in one source and Male/Female in another.

5. Duplicate Records

The same record may appear more than once after combining datasets. Duplicate detection and removal are important for accurate analysis.

Correlation Analysis

Correlation analysis helps identify relationships between attributes and can be used to investigate possible redundancy.

Pearson correlation coefficient:

$$r=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}$$

Its value ranges from -1 to +1.

  • r = +1 indicates perfect positive linear correlation.
  • r = -1 indicates perfect negative linear correlation.
  • r = 0 indicates no linear correlation.

A high correlation may suggest redundancy, but it does not prove that one attribute can always be removed. Domain knowledge and the intended mining task must also be considered.

Benefits of Data Integration

  • Creates a unified dataset.
  • Improves accessibility of information.
  • Supports cross-departmental analysis.
  • Helps discover relationships across sources.
  • Supports data warehouse construction.

children.title: Handling Redundancy, Entity Identification and Data Conflicts
children.body:
1. Redundancy Detection

Redundancy occurs when the same information is represented multiple times or an attribute can be derived from another attribute.

Example: Total_Amount may be calculated as Quantity multiplied by Unit_Price. Storing all three may introduce redundant information, depending on the application.

Methods for Detecting Redundancy

  • Check duplicate attributes across tables.
  • Identify functionally dependent attributes.
  • Use correlation analysis to find strongly related numerical attributes.
  • Apply domain knowledge to identify derivable values.

2. Entity Identification

Entity identification determines whether records from different sources refer to the same real-world object.

Example:

Database ADatabase B
Customer: Rahul NairCustomer: R. Nair
Phone: 9876543210Phone: 9876543210

Matching phone numbers and other attributes may indicate that both records represent the same customer.

Entity Resolution Process

  1. Identify candidate records.
  2. Compare relevant attributes.
  3. Calculate similarity or matching scores.
  4. Apply matching rules or thresholds.
  5. Merge confirmed matches and retain uncertain records for review.

3. Handling Data Value Conflicts

Data conflicts occur when different sources represent the same information using incompatible formats or values.

Source ASource BResolution
Height = 170 cmHeight = 1.7 mConvert to a common unit.
Gender = MGender = MaleUse a standard category.
Date = 05-06-2025Date = 2025-06-05Use a defined date format and verify interpretation.
Price = 100 USDPrice = 8500 INRConvert using an appropriate exchange rate and reference date.

4. Duplicate Detection

Duplicate detection identifies repeated records that refer to the same entity or event.

Exact matching compares all relevant fields, whereas approximate or fuzzy matching handles differences in spelling, abbreviations and formatting.

Example: An address written as 10 MG Road and 10, M. G. Road may refer to the same location.

Data Integration Checklist

  1. Identify all source systems.
  2. Understand the schema of each source.
  3. Map equivalent attributes.
  4. Resolve entity identity.
  5. Standardise formats and units.
  6. Detect and remove inappropriate duplicates.
  7. Check redundant attributes.
  8. Validate the integrated dataset.

Exam Tip

When asked about data integration problems, explain schema integration, entity identification, redundancy and data value conflicts separately, using one practical example for each.

children.title: Data Transformation: Concepts and Techniques
children.body:
Definition

Data transformation is the process of converting data from its original representation into a suitable form for data mining and analysis.

It makes data consistent, comparable and compatible with the requirements of mining algorithms.

Major Data Transformation Techniques

  1. Smoothing.
  2. Aggregation.
  3. Generalisation.
  4. Normalisation.
  5. Attribute construction.

1. Smoothing

Smoothing removes or reduces noise in data by applying techniques such as binning, regression and clustering.

Example: Replacing noisy values with bin means or medians.

2. Aggregation

Aggregation combines multiple detailed records into a summarised form.

Example: Combining daily sales into monthly sales.

DaySales
Monday1000
Tuesday1500
Wednesday1200

Weekly sales for these three days = 1000 + 1500 + 1200 = 3700.

3. Generalisation

Generalisation replaces low-level detailed values with higher-level concepts using concept hierarchies.

Example: Kochi becomes Kerala, and Kerala becomes India.

4. Normalisation

Normalisation scales numerical attributes into a common range so that attributes with different units or magnitudes can be compared.

Common techniques include min-max normalisation, z-score normalisation and decimal scaling.

5. Attribute Construction

Attribute construction creates new attributes from existing ones to improve the usefulness of data mining.

Example: Create an Age attribute from Date_of_Birth and the reference date.

Another example is creating Total_Amount from Quantity and Unit_Price:

$$\text{Total Amount}=\text{Quantity}\times\text{Unit Price}$$

Summary

TechniquePurposeExample
SmoothingReduces noise.Binning.
AggregationCombines records.Daily sales to monthly sales.
GeneralisationMoves to higher-level concepts.City to state.
NormalisationScales numerical values.Convert values to 0 to 1.
Attribute constructionCreates new attributes.Quantity multiplied by price.

children.title: Normalisation: Min-Max, Z-Score and Decimal Scaling
children.body:
Definition

Normalisation is a data transformation technique that scales numerical attribute values into a specified range or distribution.

It is useful when attributes have different scales. For example, income may be measured in thousands while age is measured in tens. Without scaling, some algorithms may be dominated by large-magnitude attributes.

1. Min-Max Normalisation

Min-max normalisation transforms an original value into a specified range, commonly [0,1].

Formula:

$$v'=\frac{v-\min(A)}{\max(A)-\min(A)}$$

For a general new range [new_min, new_max]:

$$v'=\frac{v-\min(A)}{\max(A)-\min(A)}(new\_max-new\_min)+new\_min$$

Worked Example

Given minimum = 10, maximum = 50 and value = 30, normalise the value into [0,1].

$$v'=\frac{30-10}{50-10}=\frac{20}{40}=0.5$$

Answer: 0.5.

Advantages

  • Simple to calculate.
  • Produces values in a fixed range.
  • Useful when a specific range is required.

Limitation

Highly sensitive to extreme minimum and maximum values. An outlier can compress most other values into a small interval.

2. Z-Score Normalisation

Z-score normalisation transforms values based on the mean and standard deviation of the attribute.

Formula:

$$v'=\frac{v-\mu}{\sigma}$$

Where:

  • v = Original value.
  • μ = Mean of the attribute.
  • σ = Standard deviation of the attribute.

Worked Example

Given value = 80, mean = 60 and standard deviation = 10.

$$v'=\frac{80-60}{10}=2$$

Answer: 2.

The value is two standard deviations above the mean.

Advantages

  • Does not require a fixed minimum and maximum range.
  • Useful when data contain different measurement scales.
  • Often suitable for algorithms that work with standardised numerical attributes.

Limitation

Extreme values can influence the mean and standard deviation. Z-score normalisation does not automatically remove outliers.

3. Decimal Scaling Normalisation

Decimal scaling normalises values by moving the decimal point according to the maximum absolute value.

Formula:

$$v'=\frac{v}{10^j}$$

Here, j is the smallest non-negative integer such that the maximum absolute normalised value is less than 1.

Worked Example

Dataset: 120, 450, 800.

The maximum absolute value is 800. Choose j = 3.

  • 120 / 1000 = 0.12.
  • 450 / 1000 = 0.45.
  • 800 / 1000 = 0.80.

Normalised dataset: 0.12, 0.45, 0.80.

Comparison of Normalisation Methods

MethodFormulaResult
Min-Max(v - min) / (max - min)Specified range, often 0 to 1.
Z-Score(v - mean) / standard deviationMean 0 and standard deviation 1 when population statistics are used.
Decimal Scalingv / 10^jMoves decimal point to reduce magnitude.

When to Use Each Method

  • Min-Max: When a fixed numerical range is required.
  • Z-Score: When scaling based on the distribution's mean and standard deviation is appropriate.
  • Decimal Scaling: When a simple magnitude-based scaling approach is sufficient.

Exam Practice

Question: Normalise 25 using min-max normalisation if the minimum is 5 and maximum is 45.

Solution:

$$v'=\frac{25-5}{45-5}=\frac{20}{40}=0.5$$

Question: Apply z-score normalisation to 70 if mean is 50 and standard deviation is 10.

Solution:

$$v'=\frac{70-50}{10}=2$$

children.title: Data Reduction: Need, Methods and Overview
children.body:
Definition

Data reduction is the process of obtaining a smaller representation of a dataset while preserving the essential information needed for analysis.

The reduced dataset should produce approximately the same analytical results as the original dataset for the intended task.

Why Is Data Reduction Needed?

  • Large datasets require significant storage.
  • Processing large amounts of data can be computationally expensive.
  • Some attributes may contain redundant information.
  • Data mining algorithms may become slower as the dataset grows.
  • Reducing unnecessary information can simplify analysis.

Major Data Reduction Strategies

1. Data Cube Aggregation

Summarises detailed data by combining records into higher-level aggregates.

Example: Daily sales data can be aggregated into monthly or yearly sales.

2. Attribute Subset Selection

Selects a smaller group of relevant attributes and removes irrelevant or redundant attributes.

Example: For predicting student performance, attributes such as attendance and previous marks may be useful, while an unrelated record identifier may be removed.

3. Dimensionality Reduction

Reduces the number of dimensions or attributes while preserving important information.

Common techniques include wavelet transforms and Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

4. Numerosity Reduction

Replaces the original data with a smaller representation such as a statistical model, cluster centres or compressed representation.

Methods include regression, histograms, clustering and sampling.

5. Data Compression

Encodes data using fewer bits while retaining the required information. Compression may be lossless or lossy.

Data Reduction Techniques Summary

TechniqueWhat Is Reduced?Example
Data cube aggregationLevel of detail.Daily to yearly sales.
Attribute subset selectionNumber of attributes.Remove irrelevant columns.
Dimensionality reductionNumber of dimensions.PCA.
Numerosity reductionData volume or representation size.Clustering and regression.
Data compressionStorage size.Lossless encoding.

Example

A company stores 10 million individual sales transactions. For a yearly business report, it may aggregate them into monthly sales summaries. Instead of processing every transaction for that report, the company can analyse a much smaller set of monthly records.

Important Distinction

Data reduction does not necessarily mean deleting records randomly. The objective is to reduce data size while retaining useful information and analytical quality.

children.title: Data Cube Aggregation
children.body:
Definition

Data cube aggregation is a data reduction technique in which detailed data are summarised at higher levels of a dimensional hierarchy.

It reduces the number of records that need to be processed by replacing detailed data with aggregate values.

Example

How Aggregation Works

  1. Identify the dimensions and measures.
  2. Choose the required level of detail.
  3. Group records based on the selected dimensions.
  4. Apply aggregate functions such as SUM, COUNT, AVG, MIN or MAX.
  5. Store or analyse the summarised result.

 v
Quarter
 |
 v
Year

Moving from day to month, quarter or year reduces the level of detail.

Advantages

  • Reduces the number of records used in analysis.
  • Improves performance for summary queries.
  • Supports management-level reporting.
  • Reduces repeated processing of detailed transactions.

Limitations

  • Detailed information may not be available in the aggregated representation.
  • Choosing an unsuitable aggregation level may hide important patterns.
  • Some measures cannot be directly summed, such as percentages or averages without retaining the necessary underlying statistics.

Exam Tip

Explain aggregation using a daily-to-monthly sales example. Mention the dimensions, measure and aggregation function.

children.title: Attribute Subset Selection
children.body:
Definition

Attribute subset selection is a data reduction technique that selects a relevant subset of attributes for analysis and removes irrelevant or redundant attributes.

It reduces the number of features while retaining information useful for the mining task.

Example

Consider a dataset used to predict student examination performance.

Available attributes:

  • Student ID.
  • Attendance percentage.
  • Previous examination marks.
  • Study hours.
  • Favourite colour.
  • Examination result.

Favourite colour may not contribute meaningfully to predicting examination performance. Student ID may also be unsuitable as a predictive feature. These attributes may be removed depending on the task.

Why Select Attributes?

  • Reduces dimensionality.
  • Removes irrelevant information.
  • Reduces computational cost.
  • Can improve model generalisation.
  • Improves interpretability.

Attribute Selection Methods

1. Stepwise Forward Selection

Starts with an empty set of attributes and adds the most useful attribute at each step.

  1. Start with no selected attributes.
  2. Evaluate each remaining attribute.
  3. Add the attribute that gives the best improvement.
  4. Repeat until a stopping condition is reached.

2. Stepwise Backward Elimination

Starts with all available attributes and removes the least useful attribute at each step.

  1. Start with all attributes.
  2. Evaluate the importance of each attribute.
  3. Remove the least useful attribute.
  4. Repeat until the stopping condition is reached.

3. Combination of Forward Selection and Backward Elimination

At each step, an attribute may be added or removed depending on whether it improves the selected evaluation criterion.

4. Decision Tree Induction

Decision tree algorithms select attributes that best separate the data according to a splitting criterion such as information gain or Gini index.

Forward vs Backward Selection

Forward SelectionBackward Elimination
Starts with an empty set.Starts with all attributes.
Adds attributes gradually.Removes attributes gradually.
Useful when the initial feature set is large.Can be costly when the initial feature set is very large.

Important Point

Attribute subset selection is different from creating new attributes. It selects existing attributes, whereas attribute construction creates new features from existing information.

children.title: Dimensionality Reduction and Wavelet Transform
children.body:
Definition of Dimensionality Reduction

Dimensionality reduction reduces the number of attributes or dimensions in a dataset while preserving as much important information as possible.

It helps reduce storage, computational complexity and problems caused by high-dimensional data.

Problems Caused by High Dimensionality

  • Increased computational cost.
  • Increased storage requirements.
  • Difficulty in visualising data.
  • Irrelevant dimensions may reduce model quality.
  • Distance measures can become less informative in high-dimensional spaces, a problem often associated with the curse of dimensionality.

Major Dimensionality Reduction Methods

  • Wavelet Transform.
  • Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
  • Other feature extraction and projection techniques.

Wavelet Transform

A wavelet transform represents data using wavelet coefficients at different scales and positions. It can capture both local and global patterns in data.

It is useful for compressing data and reducing dimensionality by retaining important coefficients and discarding coefficients that contribute little to the representation.

Basic Idea

  1. Apply a wavelet transform to the original data.
  2. Obtain a set of wavelet coefficients.
  3. Identify coefficients with significant contributions.
  4. Retain important coefficients and discard small or less useful coefficients according to an appropriate threshold.
  5. Use the reduced coefficient representation for further analysis.

Simple Example

Suppose a signal is represented by 1000 wavelet coefficients. If only 100 coefficients contain most of the important information, the remaining coefficients may be discarded to obtain a compact representation.

This is an illustrative example; the number of coefficients retained depends on the signal and acceptable reconstruction error.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA is a statistical dimensionality reduction technique that transforms correlated numerical attributes into a smaller set of uncorrelated variables called principal components.

The first principal component captures the maximum possible variance. Each subsequent component captures the maximum remaining variance subject to being orthogonal to the previous components.

Basic Steps of PCA

  1. Prepare the numerical dataset.
  2. Standardise attributes when appropriate.
  3. Calculate the covariance or correlation matrix.
  4. Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
  5. Rank components according to their eigenvalues.
  6. Select the required number of principal components.
  7. Project the original data onto the selected components.

Wavelet Transform vs PCA

Wavelet TransformPCA
Uses wavelet basis functions.Uses eigenvectors of covariance or correlation structure.
Captures localised patterns at different scales.Captures directions of maximum variance.
Useful for signal representation and compression.Useful for reducing correlated numerical features.
Can represent local and global signal information.Produces orthogonal principal components.

Exam Tip

Explain the objective of dimensionality reduction, the curse of dimensionality and the steps of wavelet transformation or PCA. Distinguish between feature selection and feature extraction.

children.title: Numerosity Reduction: Parametric Methods
children.body:
Definition

Numerosity reduction is a data reduction technique that replaces the original data with a smaller representation, such as a mathematical model or a compact data structure.

It reduces the amount of data that must be stored or processed.

Types of Numerosity Reduction

  • Parametric methods.
  • Non-parametric methods.

Parametric Methods

Parametric methods assume that the data can be represented using a model with a limited number of parameters. Instead of storing all original observations, the model parameters are stored.

1. Regression

Regression represents the relationship between variables using a mathematical function.

Simple Linear Regression:

$$y=a+bx$$

Where:

  • y = Predicted dependent variable.
  • x = Independent variable.
  • a = Intercept.
  • b = Slope.

Example: A company models sales based on advertising expenditure. Once the regression parameters are estimated, the model can summarise the relationship instead of storing every observation for that analytical purpose.

2. Log-Linear Models

Log-linear models are used to model multidimensional discrete data by representing relationships among variables through logarithms of expected cell frequencies.

They are useful for analysing categorical data and interactions among multiple dimensions.

Advantages of Parametric Methods

  • Can provide a compact representation of large datasets.
  • Supports prediction and estimation.
  • Can reduce storage and processing requirements.
  • Model parameters are often easier to analyse than raw data.

Limitations

  • Model assumptions may not match the actual data distribution.
  • Incorrect model selection can lead to inaccurate results.
  • Complex patterns may not be represented adequately by a simple model.

Important Point

Parametric reduction stores a model rather than the complete original data. The quality of the reduction depends on how well the model represents the underlying data.

children.title: Numerosity Reduction: Non-Parametric Methods
children.body:
Definition

Non-parametric numerosity reduction reduces data without assuming that the data follows a particular mathematical distribution or fixed parametric model.

It uses methods such as histograms, clustering and sampling to create a smaller representation.

1. Histograms

A histogram divides numerical data into intervals called buckets or bins and stores summary information for each interval.

Example: Consider ages: 18, 19, 20, 22, 25, 28, 30, 32.

Using intervals 18-21, 22-25 and 26-33:

Age IntervalFrequency
18-213
22-252
26-333

The histogram represents the distribution using a small number of intervals and frequencies.

Histogram Types

  • Equal-width: Every bucket has the same interval width.
  • Equal-frequency: Each bucket contains approximately the same number of records.

2. Clustering

Clustering divides data objects into groups based on similarity. A cluster can be represented by a centroid, medoid or other compact description.

Example: A dataset with 10000 customer records may be represented approximately using 10 cluster centres for certain analytical purposes.

Clustering-based reduction is lossy because individual records may not be recoverable from cluster representatives.

3. Sampling

Sampling selects a representative subset of records from a larger dataset.

Simple Random Sampling

Every record has an equal probability of being selected.

Sampling Without Replacement

Once a record is selected, it cannot be selected again.

Sampling With Replacement

A selected record is returned to the population and may be selected again.

Stratified Sampling

The dataset is divided into groups called strata, and samples are selected from each group.

Example: When sampling student records, select samples from each department to preserve departmental representation.

Comparison of Non-Parametric Methods

MethodBasic IdeaOutput
HistogramGroups values into intervals.Bins and frequencies.
ClusteringGroups similar objects.Clusters and representatives.
SamplingSelects a subset of records.Representative sample.

Parametric vs Non-Parametric Reduction

ParametricNon-Parametric
Assumes a model structure.Does not require a fixed parametric model.
Uses model parameters.Uses data structures or selected observations.
Examples: Regression and log-linear models.Examples: Histograms, clustering and sampling.

Exam Tip

For a numerosity reduction question, divide the answer into parametric and non-parametric methods. Explain regression and log-linear models under parametric methods, and histograms, clustering and sampling under non-parametric methods.

children.title: Data Discretization: Meaning and Need
children.body:
Definition

Data discretization is the process of converting continuous numerical attributes into a finite number of intervals or categories called bins.

Instead of representing every numerical value individually, discretization groups values into meaningful ranges.

Example

Consider the age values:

12, 18, 22, 35, 45, 60, 72

These can be converted into categories:

Age RangeCategory
0-17Child
18-35Young Adult
36-59Middle-aged
60 and aboveSenior

Need for Discretization

  • Reduces the number of distinct values.
  • Simplifies data representation.
  • Helps algorithms that work with categorical attributes.
  • Improves interpretability.
  • Can reduce the effect of small numerical variations.
  • Supports concept hierarchy generation.

Types of Discretization

1. Supervised Discretization

Uses class labels or target information when selecting interval boundaries.

Example: Selecting income ranges that best separate customers who default on loans from those who do not.

2. Unsupervised Discretization

Does not use class labels. It divides data based on the distribution of the attribute values.

Example: Dividing ages into equal-width or equal-frequency intervals.

3. Top-Down Discretization

Starts with the complete range and repeatedly splits it into smaller intervals.

4. Bottom-Up Discretization

Starts with individual values or small intervals and repeatedly merges neighbouring intervals.

Discretization Workflow

Continuous Attribute
        |
        v
Sort Values
        |
        v
Choose Number of Intervals
        |
        v
Determine Boundaries
        |
        v
Assign Values to Intervals
        |
        v
Discrete Attribute

Example

Suppose marks range from 0 to 100. A simple discretization may create the categories Low, Medium and High.

  • 0-39: Low.
  • 40-69: Medium.
  • 70-100: High.

The boundaries must be selected according to the analysis objective or an appropriate discretization method.

Advantages

  • Creates simpler representations.
  • Reduces the number of distinct numerical values.
  • Can improve interpretability.
  • May improve the efficiency of certain mining algorithms.

Limitations

  • Some numerical detail is lost.
  • Poorly selected boundaries can hide important patterns.
  • Different discretization methods may produce different results.

children.title: Discretization Methods: Binning, Histogram Analysis and Clustering
children.body:
1. Binning-Based Discretization

Binning sorts numerical values and divides them into intervals. The intervals can be created using equal-width or equal-frequency approaches.

Equal-Width Binning

Each interval has the same width.

Formula:

$$\text{Bin Width}=\frac{\max(A)-\min(A)}{k}$$

Where k is the number of bins.

Worked Example

Given values from 10 to 50, divide the range into 4 equal-width bins.

$$\text{Width}=\frac{50-10}{4}=10$$

  • Bin 1: [10,20).
  • Bin 2: [20,30).
  • Bin 3: [30,40).
  • Bin 4: [40,50].

The final interval includes the maximum value.

Equal-Frequency Binning

Each interval contains approximately the same number of observations.

Example: Sorted values: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16.

For four equal-frequency bins:

  • Bin 1: 2, 4.
  • Bin 2: 6, 8.
  • Bin 3: 10, 12.
  • Bin 4: 14, 16.

2. Histogram Analysis

Histogram analysis divides the attribute range into buckets and represents the frequency of values in each bucket.

It can be used to identify natural groupings and construct discretized intervals.

Example: A histogram of customer ages may show high frequencies in the 20-30 and 40-50 ranges. These intervals can help form useful categories.

3. Clustering-Based Discretization

Clustering groups nearby numerical values into clusters. Each cluster can be represented as an interval or category.

Example: Income values may form clusters around low-income, middle-income and high-income groups.

Unlike equal-width binning, clustering-based discretization can create intervals based on the actual data distribution.

4. Decision Tree-Based Discretization

Decision tree methods identify split points that help separate target classes. This is a supervised discretization approach.

Example: A decision tree may find that income below a certain threshold is associated with a higher probability of loan default.

Comparison

MethodBasisSupervision
Equal-width binningFixed interval width.Unsupervised.
Equal-frequency binningApproximately equal records per interval.Unsupervised.
Histogram analysisFrequency distribution.Usually unsupervised.
ClusteringSimilarity between values.Usually unsupervised.
Decision treeClass separation.Supervised.

Important Exam Points

  • Equal-width uses identical interval widths.
  • Equal-frequency uses approximately equal numbers of observations.
  • Supervised discretization uses class information.
  • Unsupervised discretization does not use class labels.

children.title: Concept Hierarchy: Meaning and Examples
children.body:
Definition

Concept hierarchy is an organisation of data values into multiple levels of abstraction, where lower-level concepts can be generalised into higher-level concepts.

It allows users to analyse data at different levels of detail.

Example 1: Location Hierarchy

Street
  |
  v
City
  |
  v
State
  |
  v
Country

Example: A street in Kochi belongs to Kochi city, which belongs to Kerala, which belongs to India.

Example 2: Time Hierarchy

Day

Month
 |
 v
Quarter
