Example 3: Product Hierarchy

Individual Product
       |
       v
Product Type
       |
       v
Product Category
       |
       v
All Products

Levels of Abstraction

  • Low-level concepts: Detailed values such as individual cities, dates or products.
  • High-level concepts: Generalised values such as states, years or product categories.

Need for Concept Hierarchy

  • Supports data generalisation.
  • Allows analysis at multiple levels.
  • Helps summarise large datasets.
  • Supports OLAP roll-up and drill-down operations.
  • Makes complex information easier to understand.

Concept Hierarchy and OLAP

Concept hierarchies provide the levels through which OLAP operations can navigate.

  • Roll-Up: Moves from a lower level to a higher level.
  • Drill-Down: Moves from a higher level to a lower level.

Example: A user can roll up daily sales into monthly sales and drill down from yearly sales into individual months.

Concept Hierarchy vs Discretization

Concept HierarchyDiscretization
Organises values into abstraction levels.Converts continuous values into discrete intervals.
May include categorical and numerical attributes.Primarily applied to numerical attributes.
Example: City to State to Country.Example: Age to age groups.

children.title: Methods of Concept Hierarchy Generation
children.body:
1. Concept Hierarchy for Categorical Attributes

Categorical attributes contain values belonging to a finite set of categories.

A hierarchy can be created using domain knowledge or relationships between categories.

Example:

City -> State -> Country

Kochi -> Kerala -> India

Trivandrum -> Kerala -> India

In this hierarchy, multiple cities are grouped under a state, and multiple states are grouped under a country.

2. Concept Hierarchy for Numerical Attributes

Numerical attributes can be organised into ranges or intervals.

Example: Age

Age
 |
 +-- 0-17: Child
 |
 +-- 18-35: Young Adult
 |
 +-- 36-59: Middle-aged
 |
 +-- 60+: Senior

Numerical intervals can be created using domain knowledge, binning, histogram analysis or other discretization techniques.

3. Automatic Generation Using Attribute Cardinality

Concept hierarchies can be generated by ordering attributes according to their number of distinct values, also called cardinality.

Attributes with more distinct values can be placed at lower levels, while attributes with fewer distinct values can be placed at higher levels, provided that a meaningful hierarchical relationship exists.

Example:

AttributeDistinct Values
StreetMany
CityFewer
StateStill fewer
CountryVery few

Possible hierarchy: Street to City to State to Country.

Important: Cardinality alone does not establish a valid hierarchy. The attributes must also have a genuine semantic relationship.

4. User-Defined Hierarchies

Domain experts can manually define hierarchies based on application requirements.

Example: A company may define a product hierarchy as individual product, product type, department and total products.

5. Hierarchy Generation Using Discretization

Continuous numerical values can be divided into intervals, and these intervals can be grouped into higher-level concepts.

Example:

Individual Age Values
       |
       v
Age Intervals
       |
       v
Age Categories
       |
       v
General Population Groups

Advantages

  • Supports data generalisation.
  • Enables multi-level analysis.
  • Reduces the complexity of detailed data.
  • Supports OLAP operations.
  • Improves the presentation of analytical results.

Exam Tip

For concept hierarchy generation, explain categorical and numerical hierarchies, attribute cardinality and user-defined hierarchies. Draw a location or time hierarchy to illustrate abstraction levels.

children.title: Important Definitions and Formula Sheet
children.body:
Important Definitions

  • Data Preprocessing: Converting raw data into a clean and suitable form for mining.
  • Data Cleaning: Detecting and correcting incomplete, inaccurate, inconsistent and noisy data.
  • Missing Values: Attribute values that are unavailable for some records.
  • Noisy Data: Data containing random errors or unwanted variations.
  • Data Integration: Combining data from multiple sources into a unified dataset.
  • Data Transformation: Converting data into a suitable representation.
  • Normalisation: Scaling numerical values into a common range or distribution.
  • Data Reduction: Producing a smaller representation while preserving useful information.
  • Attribute Subset Selection: Selecting relevant attributes and removing irrelevant or redundant ones.
  • Dimensionality Reduction: Reducing the number of dimensions while preserving important information.
  • Numerosity Reduction: Replacing original data with a compact model or representation.
  • Discretization: Converting continuous values into discrete intervals.
  • Concept Hierarchy: Organising data values into multiple levels of abstraction.

Important Formulas

1. Arithmetic Mean

$$\bar{x}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i}{n}$$

2. Min-Max Normalisation

$$v'=\frac{v-\min(A)}{\max(A)-\min(A)}$$

3. Min-Max Normalisation to a New Range

$$v'=\frac{v-\min(A)}{\max(A)-\min(A)}(new\_max-new\_min)+new\_min$$

4. Z-Score Normalisation

$$v'=\frac{v-\mu}{\sigma}$$

5. Decimal Scaling

$$v'=\frac{v}{10^j}$$

6. Equal-Width Bin Size

$$\text{Bin Width}=\frac{\max(A)-\min(A)}{k}$$

7. Pearson Correlation

$$r=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}$$

8. Linear Regression

$$y=a+bx$$

Important Comparisons

children.title: 1.1 Introduction to Classification
children.body:
Classification in Data Mining

Classification is a supervised learning technique used to assign data objects to predefined class labels or categories. A classification model learns patterns from a labelled training dataset and uses the learned patterns to predict the class of previously unseen records.

Example

Consider a dataset containing customer information such as age, income, credit score and loan repayment history. A classification model can learn to classify a new loan applicant as either Low Risk or High Risk.

Important terminology

  • Class label: The category to be predicted, such as Yes/No or Spam/Not Spam.
  • Training dataset: Labelled records used to construct the classification model.
  • Testing dataset: Records used to evaluate the model's performance.
  • Feature or attribute: An input variable used to make a prediction.
  • Classifier: The learned model that assigns class labels to new records.
  • Prediction: The class assigned by the trained classifier to an unseen record.

General classification process

  1. Collect a dataset containing records and their known class labels.
  2. Preprocess the data by handling missing values, noise and inconsistent records.
  3. Divide the dataset into training and testing portions.
  4. Apply a classification algorithm to the training dataset.
  5. Evaluate the resulting model using the testing dataset.
  6. Use the trained model to classify new records.

Types of classification

  • Binary classification: Predicts one of two classes, such as Fraud or Not Fraud.
  • Multiclass classification: Predicts one class from more than two possible classes, such as classifying a fruit as Apple, Orange or Banana.
  • Multilabel classification: Assigns multiple labels to one record, such as assigning several topics to a document.

Applications

  • Email spam detection.
  • Medical diagnosis and disease prediction.
  • Credit risk assessment.
  • Fraud detection in financial transactions.
  • Sentiment classification of customer reviews.
  • Image and document recognition.

children.title: 1.2 Decision Tree Classification
children.body:
Decision Tree

A decision tree is a supervised classification model that represents decisions and their possible outcomes in a tree-like structure. It repeatedly divides the training dataset into smaller subsets based on attribute tests until a stopping condition is reached.

Structure of a decision tree

  • Root node: Represents the first attribute test and contains the entire training dataset.
  • Internal node: Represents a test on an attribute.
  • Branch: Represents the outcome of an attribute test.
  • Leaf node: Represents the predicted class label.

Example

Consider predicting whether a person will play outside based on weather conditions.

OutlookHumidityPlay
SunnyHighNo
SunnyNormalYes
RainyHighNo
RainyNormalYes
CloudyHighYes

A decision tree may first test Outlook and then use Humidity or another attribute to determine the final class.

Decision tree construction process

  1. Start with all training records at the root node.
  2. Select the best attribute for splitting the records using a selection measure such as Information Gain or Gini Index.
  3. Create branches corresponding to the possible outcomes of the selected attribute.
  4. Divide the records among the branches.
  5. Repeat the attribute selection and splitting process recursively for each child node.
  6. Stop when a stopping condition is satisfied.
  7. Assign a class label to each leaf node, commonly using the majority class among records reaching that leaf.

Common stopping conditions

  • All records at a node belong to the same class.
  • No remaining attribute can be used for further splitting.
  • The node contains too few records to justify another split.
  • A specified maximum tree depth has been reached.
  • The improvement in the splitting measure is below a chosen threshold.

Advantages

  • Easy to understand and interpret.
  • Can handle numerical and categorical attributes.
  • Requires relatively little data preparation.
  • Can represent nonlinear decision boundaries.

Disadvantages

  • Can overfit the training data if the tree becomes too complex.
  • Small changes in training data may produce a different tree.
  • Greedy attribute selection does not guarantee a globally optimal tree.
  • Deep trees can become difficult to interpret.

children.title: 1.3 Information Gain and Entropy
children.body:
Entropy

Entropy measures the impurity or uncertainty of a dataset with respect to its class labels. It is used in decision tree algorithms to identify attributes that produce useful splits.

For a dataset S containing m classes, entropy is defined as:

$$Entropy(S)=-\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i\log_2(p_i)$$

Here, $p_i$ is the proportion of records belonging to class i.

Properties of entropy

  • Entropy is zero when all records belong to a single class.
  • Entropy is maximum when all classes are equally represented.
  • For a binary classification problem, entropy ranges from 0 to 1.
  • Higher entropy indicates greater class impurity.

Information Gain

Information Gain measures the reduction in entropy obtained by splitting a dataset using an attribute. It measures how effectively an attribute separates records into their respective classes.

For an attribute A:

$$Gain(S,A)=Entropy(S)-\sum_{v\in Values(A)}\frac{|S_v|}{|S|}Entropy(S_v)$$

Where:

  • $S$ is the original dataset.
  • $A$ is the attribute being evaluated.
  • $Values(A)$ is the set of possible values of A.
  • $S_v$ is the subset of records for which attribute A has value v.
  • $|S_v|/|S|$ is the proportion of records in that subset.

The attribute with the highest Information Gain is selected for splitting in ID3.

Numerical example

Consider a dataset with 10 records: 6 belong to class Yes and 4 belong to class No.

Initial entropy:

$$Entropy(S)=-\frac{6}{10}\log_2\frac{6}{10}-\frac{4}{10}\log_2\frac{4}{10}$$

$$Entropy(S)\approx 0.971$$

Suppose an attribute divides the records into two subsets:

  • Subset 1: 4 Yes and 0 No, with entropy 0.
  • Subset 2: 2 Yes and 4 No, with entropy approximately 0.918.

Weighted entropy after splitting:

$$Entropy_{split}=\frac{4}{10}(0)+\frac{6}{10}(0.918)$$

$$Entropy_{split}\approx 0.551$$

Information Gain:

$$Gain(S,A)=0.971-0.551=0.420$$

Therefore, the attribute provides approximately 0.420 bits of information gain.

Important points

  • Information Gain is based on entropy.
  • A higher Information Gain indicates a better split according to this criterion.
  • Information Gain can favour attributes with many distinct values.
  • Information Gain is the attribute selection measure used by ID3.

children.title: 1.4 Gini Index
children.body:
Gini Index

The Gini Index is an impurity measure used to evaluate the quality of a split in a decision tree. It estimates the probability of incorrectly classifying a randomly selected record if its class label is assigned according to the class distribution at a node.

For a dataset S containing m classes:

$$Gini(S)=1-\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i^2$$

Where $p_i$ is the proportion of records belonging to class i.

Properties

  • Gini Index is zero when all records belong to one class.
  • A lower Gini value indicates a purer dataset.
  • For two equally represented classes, Gini reaches its maximum value of 0.5.
  • For a split, the weighted Gini impurity of the child nodes is calculated.

Gini Index after splitting

For an attribute A that produces k subsets:

$$Gini_{split}(S,A)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\frac{|S_j|}{|S|}Gini(S_j)$$

The split with the lowest weighted Gini impurity is preferred.

Numerical example

Consider a dataset containing 10 records: 6 Yes and 4 No.

$$Gini(S)=1-\left(\frac{6}{10}\right)^2-\left(\frac{4}{10}\right)^2$$

$$Gini(S)=1-0.36-0.16=0.48$$

Suppose a split produces two subsets:

  • Subset 1: 4 Yes and 0 No. Its Gini Index is 0.
  • Subset 2: 2 Yes and 4 No. Its Gini Index is $1-(2/6)^2-(4/6)^2\approx 0.444$.

Weighted Gini impurity:

$$Gini_{split}=\frac{4}{10}(0)+\frac{6}{10}(0.444)$$

$$Gini_{split}\approx 0.267$$

The split reduces impurity from 0.48 to approximately 0.267.

Information Gain versus Gini Index

Information GainGini Index
Uses entropy to measure impurity.Uses squared class probabilities to measure impurity.
Chooses the attribute with the highest gain.Chooses the split with the lowest weighted Gini impurity.
Uses logarithmic calculations.Uses squared probabilities and avoids logarithms.
Used by ID3.Commonly used by CART decision trees.

children.title: 1.5 ID3 Decision Tree Algorithm
children.body:
ID3 Algorithm

ID3 stands for Iterative Dichotomiser 3. It is a decision tree learning algorithm developed by Ross Quinlan. ID3 constructs a decision tree using a top-down, greedy approach and selects attributes based on Information Gain.

Working principle

At each stage, ID3 chooses the attribute that gives the maximum reduction in entropy. The dataset is then divided according to the selected attribute's possible values. The process continues recursively until the records at a node belong to the same class or no useful attribute remains.

Algorithm steps

  1. Begin with the complete labelled training dataset as the root dataset.
  2. If all records belong to the same class, create a leaf node with that class.
  3. If no attributes remain for splitting, create a leaf node containing the majority class.
  4. Calculate the entropy of the current dataset.
  5. Calculate the Information Gain for every available attribute.
  6. Select the attribute with the highest Information Gain.
  7. Create a decision node for the selected attribute.
  8. For each possible attribute value, create a branch and form the corresponding subset.
  9. Apply ID3 recursively to each subset using the remaining attributes.
  10. Return the completed decision tree.

Pseudocode

ID3(S, Attributes):
    if all records in S belong to the same class:
        return leaf containing that class

    if Attributes is empty:
        return leaf containing majority class in S

    A = attribute with maximum Information Gain
    create decision node for A

    for each value v of A:
        Sv = records in S where A = v

        if Sv is empty:
            attach majority-class leaf to branch v
        else:
            attach ID3(Sv, Attributes - {A}) to branch v

    return decision node

Characteristics of ID3

  • Uses Information Gain for attribute selection.
  • Builds the tree recursively from the root downward.
  • Uses a greedy selection strategy at each node.
  • Original ID3 is primarily designed for categorical attributes.
  • Original ID3 does not include a built-in pruning procedure.

Limitations

  • Can overfit noisy training data.
  • Information Gain may favour attributes with many distinct values.
  • Original ID3 does not directly handle continuous attributes without suitable discretization or extensions.
  • Missing attribute values require additional handling.

Related algorithms

  • C4.5: Extends ID3 with features such as Gain Ratio, handling continuous attributes and pruning.
  • CART: Builds classification or regression trees and commonly uses Gini impurity for classification splits.

children.title: 1.6 Overfitting and Pruning in Decision Trees
children.body:
Overfitting

Overfitting occurs when a decision tree learns the training data too closely, including noise and accidental patterns. Such a tree may achieve very high training accuracy but perform poorly on unseen data.

Causes

  • Excessive tree depth.
  • Too many branches and leaf nodes.
  • Small training subsets at leaf nodes.
  • Noise and irrelevant attributes in the training dataset.

Pruning

Pruning is the process of reducing the size of a decision tree by removing branches that provide little predictive value. It helps reduce overfitting and can improve generalization.

Types of pruning

  • Pre-pruning: Stops tree growth early when a stopping condition is reached. Examples include limiting maximum depth, requiring a minimum number of records in a node, or requiring a minimum impurity reduction.
  • Post-pruning: First builds a larger tree and then removes branches that do not improve performance on validation data or according to a complexity criterion.

Benefits of pruning

  • Reduces model complexity.
  • Can improve performance on unseen records.
  • Produces a simpler and more interpretable tree.
  • Reduces the effect of noise in the training dataset.

children.title: 2.1 Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks
children.body:
Artificial Neural Network

An Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is a computational model inspired by the way biological neural systems process information. It consists of interconnected processing units called neurons, arranged in layers. Neural networks learn relationships between input features and output values by adjusting connection weights during training.

Basic structure

  • Input layer: Receives the input features from the dataset.
  • Hidden layer: Processes inputs through weighted connections and activation functions. A network may contain one or more hidden layers.
  • Output layer: Produces the final prediction, such as a class probability or predicted value.
  • Weights: Numerical values that determine the strength of connections between neurons.
  • Bias: An additional learnable parameter that shifts a neuron's weighted input.
  • Activation function: Transforms a neuron's weighted input into its output.

Artificial neuron model

A neuron receives inputs, multiplies each input by its corresponding weight, adds a bias and applies an activation function.

$$z=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_ix_i+b$$

$$y=f(z)$$

Where:

  • $x_i$ is the i-th input.
  • $w_i$ is the corresponding weight.
  • $b$ is the bias.
  • $f$ is the activation function.
  • $y$ is the neuron output.

Common activation functions

1. Sigmoid:

$$f(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$$

Produces values between 0 and 1. It is commonly used for binary classification output probabilities, although it can suffer from vanishing gradients in deep networks.

2. Tanh:

$$f(x)=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{e^x+e^{-x}}$$

Produces values between -1 and 1. Its output is zero-centred, but it can also suffer from vanishing gradients.

3. ReLU:

$$f(x)=\max(0,x)$$

Produces zero for negative inputs and the input itself for positive inputs. It is widely used in hidden layers.

4. Softmax:

$$f(z_i)=\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}$$

Converts a vector of output scores into values that sum to one. It is commonly used for mutually exclusive multiclass classification.

Applications

  • Image and speech recognition.
  • Medical diagnosis.
  • Text classification.
  • Fraud detection.
  • Pattern recognition and forecasting.

children.title: 2.2 Feedforward Neural Networks
children.body:
Feedforward Neural Network

A feedforward neural network is an ANN in which information moves from the input layer through hidden layers to the output layer without forming cycles or feedback connections.

Working

  1. The input layer receives feature values.
  2. Each neuron calculates a weighted sum of its inputs and adds a bias.
  3. An activation function is applied to the weighted sum.
  4. The resulting values are passed to the next layer.
  5. The output layer produces the final prediction.

Forward propagation equations

For layer l:

$$z^{(l)}=W^{(l)}a^{(l-1)}+b^{(l)}$$

$$a^{(l)}=f(z^{(l)})$$

Where $W^{(l)}$ represents the weight matrix, $b^{(l)}$ represents the bias vector, $a^{(l-1)}$ is the previous layer's output, and $f$ is the activation function.

Example

Suppose a neural network receives two inputs, study hours and attendance, and predicts whether a student will pass. The input values travel through hidden neurons, where weights and activation functions transform them. The output neuron produces the predicted probability of passing.

Important points

  • Information moves in one direction from input to output.
  • Weights and biases are learned during training.
  • Nonlinear activation functions allow the network to learn complex relationships.
  • Feedforward propagation calculates predictions, while backpropagation calculates gradients for learning.

children.title: 2.3 Backpropagation Algorithm
children.body:
Backpropagation

Backpropagation is a supervised learning procedure used to train multilayer neural networks. It calculates the gradients of the loss function with respect to the network's weights and biases by propagating errors backward from the output layer towards the input layer.

The calculated gradients are used by an optimization algorithm, such as gradient descent, to update the network parameters and reduce prediction error.

Main stages

  1. Initialization: Initialize weights and biases, usually with small values using a suitable initialization method.
  2. Forward propagation: Pass the input through the network and calculate the output.
  3. Loss calculation: Compare the predicted output with the actual target using a loss function.
  4. Backward propagation: Apply the chain rule to calculate gradients of the loss with respect to weights and biases.
  5. Parameter update: Update weights and biases using an optimization algorithm.
  6. Iteration: Repeat the process for multiple training examples and epochs until a stopping condition is reached.

Gradient descent update rule

$$w_{new}=w_{old}-\eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}$$

$$b_{new}=b_{old}-\eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}$$

Where:

  • $L$ is the loss function.
  • $\eta$ is the learning rate.
  • $\partial L/\partial w$ is the gradient of the loss with respect to a weight.
  • $\partial L/\partial b$ is the gradient of the loss with respect to a bias.

Backpropagation for a simple output neuron

For an output neuron with sigmoid activation and binary cross-entropy loss, the output error term can be written as:

$$\delta=\hat{y}-y$$

Here, $\hat{y}$ is the predicted probability and $y$ is the actual binary target. For a weight connecting input activation $a_i$ to the output neuron:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_i}=\delta a_i$$

For a hidden layer, the error is calculated by propagating the next layer's error backward through the weights and multiplying by the derivative of the hidden layer's activation function.

General hidden-layer error term

$$\delta^{(l)}=\left((W^{(l+1)})^T\delta^{(l+1)}\right)\odot f'(z^{(l)})$$

Here, $\odot$ represents element-wise multiplication and $f'$ is the derivative of the activation function.

Important parameters

  • Learning rate: Controls the size of each parameter update. A very high value may cause unstable training, while a very low value may make learning slow.
  • Epoch: One complete pass through the training dataset.
  • Batch: A subset of training records used for one parameter update.
  • Loss function: Measures the difference between predicted and actual outputs.
  • Gradient: Indicates the direction and rate of change of the loss with respect to a parameter.

Advantages

  • Can train multilayer neural networks.
  • Can learn complex nonlinear relationships.
  • Uses gradients to systematically reduce prediction error.
  • Can be applied to classification and regression tasks.

Limitations

  • Training can be computationally expensive.
  • Performance depends on network architecture and hyperparameter choices.
  • Deep networks can experience vanishing or exploding gradients.
  • May overfit when training data is limited or regularization is insufficient.
  • Learned models can be difficult to interpret.

children.title: 2.4 Loss Functions and Neural Network Training
children.body:
Loss Functions

A loss function measures the difference between a neural network's predicted output and the actual target. Training aims to minimize this loss by adjusting weights and biases.

Mean Squared Error

Mean Squared Error is commonly used for regression tasks.

$$MSE=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2$$

Binary Cross-Entropy

Binary cross-entropy is used for binary classification when the model produces a probability for one of two classes.

$$L=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[y_i\log(\hat{y}_i)+(1-y_i)\log(1-\hat{y}_i)]$$

Categorical Cross-Entropy

Categorical cross-entropy is commonly used for mutually exclusive multiclass classification.

$$L=-\sum_{i=1}^{C}y_i\log(\hat{y}_i)$$

Here, C is the number of classes, $y_i$ is the target indicator for class i and $\hat{y}_i$ is the predicted probability for class i.

Training considerations

  • Normalize or standardize input features when appropriate.
  • Choose an appropriate architecture and activation functions.
  • Select a suitable loss function for the task.
  • Use a validation dataset to monitor generalization.
  • Use regularization, dropout or early stopping when appropriate to reduce overfitting.
  • Evaluate the final model on a separate test dataset.

children.title: 3.1 Confusion Matrix
children.body:
Confusion Matrix

A confusion matrix is a table used to evaluate a classification model by comparing predicted class labels with actual class labels. For binary classification, it contains four outcomes.

Actual / PredictedPredicted PositivePredicted Negative
Actual PositiveTrue Positive (TP)False Negative (FN)
Actual NegativeFalse Positive (FP)True Negative (TN)

Terms

  • True Positive (TP): The model correctly predicts the positive class.
  • True Negative (TN): The model correctly predicts the negative class.
  • False Positive (FP): The model predicts positive when the actual class is negative. Also called a Type I error.
  • False Negative (FN): The model predicts negative when the actual class is positive. Also called a Type II error.

Example

A disease detection model is tested on 100 people. It produces the following results:

  • TP = 40
  • TN = 50
  • FP = 5
  • FN = 5

The model correctly classifies 40 people with the disease and 50 people without the disease. It incorrectly identifies 5 healthy people as positive and misses 5 people who have the disease.

children.title: 3.2 Accuracy, Error Rate, Precision and Recall
children.body:
Classification Evaluation Metrics

1. Accuracy

Accuracy measures the proportion of all predictions that are correct.

$$Accuracy=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}$$

Using the previous example:

$$Accuracy=\frac{40+50}{100}=0.90=90\%$$

2. Error Rate

Error Rate measures the proportion of incorrect predictions.

$$Error\ Rate=\frac{FP+FN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}$$

$$Error\ Rate=\frac{5+5}{100}=10\%$$

3. Precision

Precision measures how many records predicted as positive are actually positive.

$$Precision=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}$$

$$Precision=\frac{40}{40+5}=0.889=88.89\%$$

High precision is important when false positive predictions are costly.

4. Recall or Sensitivity

Recall measures how many actual positive records are correctly identified.

$$Recall=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}$$

$$Recall=\frac{40}{40+5}=0.889=88.89\%$$

High recall is important when missing a positive case is costly, such as in disease screening.

5. Specificity

Specificity measures how many actual negative records are correctly identified.

$$Specificity=\frac{TN}{TN+FP}$$

$$Specificity=\frac{50}{50+5}=0.909=90.91\%$$

6. F1-Score

F1-Score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

$$F1=2\times\frac{Precision\times Recall}{Precision+Recall}$$

For the example, precision and recall are both approximately 0.889, so the F1-Score is approximately 0.889 or 88.89%.

Why accuracy alone may be misleading

Consider a dataset containing 990 negative records and only 10 positive records. A classifier that predicts every record as negative achieves 99% accuracy, but it fails to identify any positive record. Precision, recall, the confusion matrix and other suitable measures are therefore necessary, especially for imbalanced datasets.

children.title: 3.3 ROC Curve and AUC
children.body:
ROC Curve

The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve evaluates a binary classifier at different classification thresholds. It plots the True Positive Rate against the False Positive Rate.

$$TPR=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}$$

$$FPR=\frac{FP}{FP+TN}$$

TPR is the same as recall or sensitivity. FPR is the proportion of actual negative records incorrectly classified as positive.

Area Under the Curve

AUC is the area under the ROC curve. It summarizes the classifier's ability to rank positive examples above negative examples across different thresholds.

  • AUC = 1: Perfect ranking performance.
  • AUC = 0.5: Performance equivalent to random ranking, under the standard interpretation.
  • AUC below 0.5: Ranking is worse than random and may indicate reversed predictions or a poor model.

Uses

  • Comparing binary classifiers.
  • Evaluating models across different decision thresholds.
  • Assessing ranking performance when a single threshold is not fixed.

Limitations

  • ROC-AUC may appear strong even when performance on a rare positive class is inadequate.
  • It does not directly specify the best operating threshold.
  • Precision-recall analysis can be more informative for highly imbalanced datasets.

children.title: 3.4 Training, Validation and Testing
children.body:
Dataset Splitting

To evaluate a classifier fairly, data is commonly divided into training, validation and testing subsets.

  • Training set: Used to learn model parameters.
  • Validation set: Used to select hyperparameters, compare model configurations and monitor overfitting.
  • Test set: Used for final evaluation after model selection is complete.

Common splitting example

A dataset may be divided into 70% training, 15% validation and 15% testing records. These percentages are illustrative; the appropriate split depends on dataset size and the task.

Cross-validation

In k-fold cross-validation, the dataset is divided into k approximately equal folds. The model is trained k times. In each iteration, one fold is used for validation and the remaining k-1 folds are used for training. The performance scores are then averaged.

Benefits of cross-validation

  • Uses multiple training and validation partitions.
  • Provides a more stable estimate of model performance than relying on one split alone.
  • Helps compare models and select hyperparameters.

Important precautions

  • Do not use the test set to tune the model.
  • Use stratified splitting when class proportions need to be preserved.
  • Perform preprocessing steps such as scaling and feature selection using training data only, then apply the learned transformations to validation and test data.
  • For time-dependent data, use a time-aware split rather than randomly mixing past and future observations.

children.title: 4.1 Introduction to Clustering
children.body:
Clustering in Data Mining

Clustering is an unsupervised learning technique that groups data objects based on their similarity. Objects within the same cluster should be more similar to one another than to objects in other clusters, according to the selected similarity or distance measure.

Characteristics

  • Does not require predefined class labels.
  • Discovers hidden structures and patterns in data.
  • Groups records based on their features and a similarity measure.
  • Results depend on the algorithm, distance measure and parameter settings.

Applications

  • Customer segmentation.
  • Grouping news articles and documents.
  • Image segmentation.
  • Grouping similar biological samples.
  • Detecting unusual records and potential outliers.
  • Geographical and spatial data analysis.

Classification versus clustering

ClassificationClustering
Supervised learning.Unsupervised learning.
Uses labelled training data.Does not require predefined class labels.
Predicts predefined classes.Discovers groups in the data.
Examples include ID3 and neural networks.Examples include k-means, hierarchical clustering and DBSCAN.

Similarity and distance measures

Clustering algorithms commonly use distance or similarity measures to compare records.

Euclidean distance:

$$d(x,y)=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-y_i)^2}$$

Manhattan distance:

$$d(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_i-y_i|$$

Minkowski distance:

$$d(x,y)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_i-y_i|^p\right)^{1/p}$$

When p = 1, Minkowski distance becomes Manhattan distance. When p = 2, it becomes Euclidean distance.

Importance of feature scaling

Distance-based clustering can be dominated by features with large numerical ranges. Normalization or standardization is often required so that features contribute more comparably to distance calculations.

children.title: 4.2 K-Means Clustering
children.body:
K-Means Algorithm

K-means is a partition-based clustering algorithm that divides a dataset into a specified number of clusters, k. Each record is assigned to the cluster whose centroid is nearest according to the selected distance measure, commonly Euclidean distance.

Centroid

A centroid is the mean position of all data points assigned to a cluster. For a cluster containing n points in d dimensions:

$$\mu=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i$$

The centroid is calculated separately for each feature by taking its arithmetic mean across the cluster's records.

Objective function

K-means aims to minimize the within-cluster sum of squared distances:

$$J=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{x_i\in C_j}||x_i-\mu_j||^2$$

Where $C_j$ is cluster j and $\mu_j$ is its centroid.

Algorithm steps

  1. Choose the number of clusters k.
  2. Initialize k centroids, commonly by selecting data points or using k-means++ initialization.
  3. Calculate the distance between every data point and each centroid.
  4. Assign each data point to its nearest centroid.
  5. Recalculate each centroid as the mean of the points assigned to that cluster.
  6. Repeat the assignment and centroid update steps.
  7. Stop when assignments no longer change, centroid movement is sufficiently small, or a maximum iteration limit is reached.

Simple example

Consider six one-dimensional points: 2, 4, 5, 10, 12 and 14. Let k = 2 and choose initial centroids 2 and 10.

  • Points 2, 4 and 5 are assigned to the first cluster.
  • Points 10, 12 and 14 are assigned to the second cluster.

New centroids:

$$\mu_1=\frac{2+4+5}{3}=3.67$$

$$\mu_2=\frac{10+12+14}{3}=12$$

The assignment and centroid update steps are repeated until the clusters stabilize.

Advantages

  • Simple to understand and implement.
  • Efficient for many numerical datasets.
  • Works well when clusters are compact and approximately spherical.
  • Easy to interpret using cluster centroids.

Disadvantages

  • The number of clusters k must be selected in advance.
  • Results can depend on initial centroid selection.
  • Sensitive to outliers because means are affected by extreme values.
  • May converge to a local minimum rather than the global minimum.
  • Not suitable for arbitrary-shaped clusters.
  • Standard k-means is primarily designed for numerical features.

Choosing k

The elbow method is commonly used to help choose k. Run k-means for different values of k and plot the within-cluster sum of squares against k. Select a value near the point where the reduction in error begins to slow noticeably. The elbow is a heuristic and may not be clearly visible.

K-means++

K-means++ is an initialization method that selects initial centroids with a preference for points that are far from already selected centroids. It often improves initialization quality and reduces the chance of poor clustering results.

children.title: 4.3 Hierarchical Clustering
children.body:
Hierarchical Clustering

Hierarchical clustering creates a hierarchy of nested clusters. The result is commonly represented using a tree-like diagram called a dendrogram. Unlike standard k-means, hierarchical clustering does not require the number of clusters to be fixed before the hierarchy is constructed.

Types of hierarchical clustering

1. Agglomerative clustering: A bottom-up approach. Initially, each data point forms its own cluster. The closest clusters are repeatedly merged until all points belong to one cluster or a stopping condition is reached.

2. Divisive clustering: A top-down approach. Initially, all data points belong to one cluster. The cluster is repeatedly divided into smaller clusters.

Agglomerative algorithm steps

  1. Start with each data point as an individual cluster.
  2. Calculate the distances between clusters.
  3. Identify the two closest clusters.
  4. Merge the selected clusters.
  5. Update the distances between the new cluster and the remaining clusters using a linkage method.
  6. Repeat until the required hierarchy or stopping condition is reached.
  7. Cut the dendrogram at a selected height to obtain the desired clusters.

Linkage methods

Linkage defines how the distance between two clusters is calculated.

  • Single linkage: Uses the minimum distance between any point in one cluster and any point in the other cluster.
  • Complete linkage: Uses the maximum distance between any point in one cluster and any point in the other cluster.
  • Average linkage: Uses the average of all pairwise distances between points in the two clusters.
  • Centroid linkage: Uses the distance between the centroids of the two clusters.
  • Ward's method: Merges the pair of clusters that produces the smallest increase in within-cluster sum of squares.

Dendrogram

A dendrogram is a tree diagram that displays the sequence and distance levels at which clusters are merged or divided. The vertical height of a merge commonly represents the dissimilarity at which two clusters are joined. Cutting the dendrogram at a chosen height determines the resulting cluster groups.

Advantages

  • Does not require the number of clusters to be specified before constructing the hierarchy.
  • Provides a visual representation of nested cluster relationships.
  • Can use different distance and linkage measures.
  • Useful for discovering hierarchical structure in data.

Disadvantages

  • Can be computationally expensive for large datasets.
  • Early merging or splitting decisions are generally not reversed.
  • Results can be sensitive to distance and linkage choices.
  • Noise and outliers may affect the resulting hierarchy.

Agglomerative versus divisive clustering

AgglomerativeDivisive
Bottom-up approach.Top-down approach.
Starts with individual data points as clusters.Starts with all data points in one cluster.
Repeatedly merges clusters.Repeatedly splits clusters.
Commonly used in practice.Often more computationally demanding depending on the splitting method.

children.title: 4.4 DBSCAN Clustering
children.body:
DBSCAN

DBSCAN stands for Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise. It is a density-based clustering algorithm that groups closely packed points and identifies points in low-density regions as noise or outliers.

Unlike k-means, DBSCAN does not require the number of clusters to be specified in advance and can identify clusters with irregular shapes.

Important parameters

  • Epsilon (ε): The maximum distance used to define the neighbourhood of a point.
  • MinPts: The minimum number of points required within the ε-neighbourhood for a point to be considered a core point. Implementations commonly count the point itself in its neighbourhood.

Types of points

  • Core point: A point having at least MinPts points in its ε-neighbourhood.
  • Border point: A point that has fewer than MinPts points in its own ε-neighbourhood but lies within the ε-neighbourhood of a core point.
  • Noise point: A point that is neither a core point nor a border point of any cluster.

Important concepts

  • Directly density-reachable: A point q is directly density-reachable from a core point p when q lies within p's ε-neighbourhood.
  • Density-reachable: A point can be reached from another point through a chain of directly density-reachable points, subject to the core-point condition.
  • Density-connected: Two points are density-connected when there is a point from which both are density-reachable.

Algorithm steps

  1. Choose ε and MinPts.
  2. Select an unvisited point.
  3. Find all points within its ε-neighbourhood.
  4. If the neighbourhood contains fewer than MinPts points, mark the point as noise temporarily.
  5. If it contains at least MinPts points, identify it as a core point and create a new cluster.
  6. Expand the cluster by adding its density-reachable points.
  7. For every newly discovered core point, include the points in its ε-neighbourhood and continue expansion.
  8. Repeat until all points have been visited.
  9. Points not assigned to any cluster remain classified as noise.

Advantages

  • Does not require the number of clusters in advance.
  • Can discover clusters with irregular shapes.
  • Can identify noise and outliers.
  • Does not rely on calculating cluster centroids.

Disadvantages

  • Choosing suitable ε and MinPts values can be difficult.
  • Performance can degrade when clusters have significantly different densities.
  • Distance calculations become less meaningful in high-dimensional spaces.
  • Results depend on the distance measure and feature scaling.

Choosing parameters

The k-distance graph can help select ε. For each point, calculate the distance to its k-th nearest neighbour, where k is commonly related to MinPts. Sort these distances and plot them. A noticeable bend in the graph can suggest a useful ε value. This is a heuristic, not a guaranteed optimum.

children.title: 4.5 Comparison of K-Means, Hierarchical Clustering and DBSCAN
children.body:
Clustering Algorithm Comparison

ApproachCentroid-based partitioningHierarchical merging or splittingDensity-based clustering
Number of clustersMust be specified as kChosen by cutting the dendrogramNot required in advance
Cluster shapeWorks best with compact, roughly spherical clustersDepends on distance and linkage methodCan find irregularly shaped clusters
Noise handlingSensitive to outliersCan be affected by outliersExplicitly identifies noise points
Main parametersNumber of clusters kDistance measure, linkage method and cut levelε and MinPts

Typical limitationSensitive to initialization and outliersCan be expensive on large datasetsDifficulty with varying densities and high dimensions

When to use each algorithm

  • K-means: Suitable when the dataset is numerical, clusters are relatively compact and the number of clusters is known or can be estimated.
  • Hierarchical clustering: Suitable when the hierarchy among groups is important and a dendrogram is useful for analysis.
  • DBSCAN: Suitable when clusters may have irregular shapes and the dataset contains noise or outliers.

children.title: 4.6 Evaluation of Clustering Results
children.body:
Clustering Evaluation

Clustering evaluation measures how well a clustering algorithm groups data. Since clustering is generally unsupervised, evaluation may use internal measures based on the data itself or external measures based on known reference labels.

1. Within-Cluster Sum of Squares

Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) measures the sum of squared distances between data points and their assigned cluster centroids.

$$WCSS=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{x_i\in C_j}||x_i-\mu_j||^2$$

Lower WCSS indicates that points are closer to their cluster centroids. However, WCSS generally decreases as the number of clusters increases, so it should not be interpreted alone.

2. Silhouette Coefficient

The silhouette coefficient measures how well a point fits within its own cluster compared with the nearest alternative cluster.

For a point i:

  • $a(i)$ is the average distance from i to other points in its own cluster.
  • $b(i)$ is the smallest average distance from i to points in another cluster.

$$s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max(a(i),b(i))}$$

The silhouette coefficient ranges from -1 to 1.

  • Close to 1: The point is well matched to its own cluster.
  • Close to 0: The point lies near a cluster boundary.
  • Below 0: The point may be assigned to an unsuitable cluster.

3. External evaluation

When reference class labels are available, clustering results can be compared with those labels using external measures such as purity, adjusted Rand index and normalized mutual information.

Purity

Purity measures the extent to which each cluster contains records from a dominant reference class.

$$Purity=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k}\max_j|C_k\cap L_j|$$

Here, $C_k$ is a cluster, $L_j$ is a reference class and N is the total number of records. Higher purity indicates better agreement with the reference classes, but purity can increase simply by creating more clusters.

Important evaluation considerations

  • Use more than one evaluation measure when possible.
  • Consider whether the chosen distance measure is appropriate for the data.
  • Check whether clusters are meaningful for the intended application.
  • Do not assume that a high numerical score automatically means the clusters are useful.

children.title: 5.1 Important Formula Sheet
children.body:
Classification Formulas

Entropy:

$$Entropy(S)=-\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i\log_2(p_i)$$

Information Gain:

$$Gain(S,A)=Entropy(S)-\sum_v\frac{|S_v|}{|S|}Entropy(S_v)$$

Gini Index:

$$Gini(S)=1-\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i^2$$

Weighted Gini after splitting:

$$Gini_{split}(S,A)=\sum_j\frac{|S_j|}{|S|}Gini(S_j)$$

Accuracy:

$$Accuracy=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}$$

Error Rate:

$$Error\ Rate=\frac{FP+FN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}$$

Precision:

$$Precision=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}$$

Recall:

$$Recall=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}$$

Specificity:

$$Specificity=\frac{TN}{TN+FP}$$

F1-Score:

$$F1=2\times\frac{Precision\times Recall}{Precision+Recall}$$

True Positive Rate:

$$TPR=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}$$

False Positive Rate:

$$FPR=\frac{FP}{FP+TN}$$

Neural Network Formulas

Neuron weighted input:

$$z=\sum_iw_ix_i+b$$

Neuron output:

$$y=f(z)$$

Gradient descent update:

$$w_{new}=w_{old}-\eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}$$

Sigmoid:

$$f(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$$

ReLU:

$$f(x)=\max(0,x)$$

Clustering Formulas

Euclidean distance:

$$d(x,y)=\sqrt{\sum_i(x_i-y_i)^2}$$

Manhattan distance:

$$d(x,y)=\sum_i|x_i-y_i|$$

K-means centroid:

$$\mu_j=\frac{1}{|C_j|}\sum_{x_i\in C_j}x_i$$

K-means objective:

$$J=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{x_i\in C_j}||x_i-\mu_j||^2$$

Silhouette coefficient:

$$s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max(a(i),b(i))}$$
