modules.title: Module 4: Association Rule Analysis and Advanced Data Mining
modules.subtitle: PECST525 | Data Mining

children.title: 1.1 Introduction to Association Rule Mining
children.body:
Association Rule Mining

Association Rule Mining is a data mining technique used to discover interesting relationships, associations and patterns among items in large datasets. It identifies items that frequently occur together and expresses these relationships as rules.

It is commonly applied to transactional databases, where each transaction contains a set of purchased items.

Example

Consider a supermarket transaction database. Customers who purchase bread and butter may frequently purchase milk as well. An association rule can represent this relationship as:

$$\{Bread, Butter\}\Rightarrow\{Milk\}$$

This means that transactions containing bread and butter are often associated with milk. It does not necessarily mean that purchasing bread and butter causes a customer to purchase milk.

Basic terminology

  • Item: An individual product or attribute, such as bread, milk or butter.
  • Itemset: A collection of one or more items.
  • Transaction: A record containing a set of items.
  • Transaction database: A collection of transactions.
  • Frequent itemset: An itemset whose support is greater than or equal to a specified minimum support threshold.
  • Association rule: An implication of the form $X\Rightarrow Y$, where X and Y are itemsets and $X\cap Y=\emptyset$.

Applications

  • Market basket analysis in retail stores.
  • Product recommendation systems.
  • Cross-selling and product placement.
  • Website navigation pattern analysis.
  • Medical diagnosis and symptom association analysis.
  • Analysis of customer purchasing behaviour.

Association rule mining process

  1. Collect transactional data.
  2. Identify frequent itemsets using a minimum support threshold.
  3. Generate association rules from the frequent itemsets.
  4. Calculate confidence and other interestingness measures.
  5. Retain rules that satisfy the selected thresholds and are useful for the application.

children.title: 1.2 Support, Confidence and Lift
children.body:
Measures for Association Rules

Association rules are evaluated using measures that indicate how frequently itemsets occur and how strongly items are associated.

1. Support

Support measures the proportion of transactions that contain an itemset.

For an itemset X:

$$Support(X)=\frac{\text{Number of transactions containing X}}{\text{Total number of transactions}}$$

For a rule $X\Rightarrow Y$:

$$Support(X\Rightarrow Y)=Support(X\cup Y)$$

Support indicates how frequently the complete combination occurs in the database.

2. Confidence

Confidence measures how often transactions containing X also contain Y. It is the conditional probability of Y occurring given X.

$$Confidence(X\Rightarrow Y)=\frac{Support(X\cup Y)}{Support(X)}$$

High confidence indicates that Y frequently occurs in transactions containing X. However, confidence alone does not establish whether the relationship is stronger than expected by chance.

3. Lift

Lift measures how much more frequently X and Y occur together compared with what would be expected if they were statistically independent.

$$Lift(X\Rightarrow Y)=\frac{Confidence(X\Rightarrow Y)}{Support(Y)}$$

Equivalently:

$$Lift(X\Rightarrow Y)=\frac{Support(X\cup Y)}{Support(X)\times Support(Y)}$$

  • Lift greater than 1: Positive association. X and Y occur together more often than expected under independence.
  • Lift equal to 1: X and Y are statistically independent according to this measure.
  • Lift less than 1: Negative association. X and Y occur together less often than expected under independence.

Numerical example

Consider 100 supermarket transactions:

  • 40 transactions contain bread.
  • 50 transactions contain milk.
  • 30 transactions contain both bread and milk.

Support of the rule Bread → Milk:

$$Support=\frac{30}{100}=0.30=30\%$$

Confidence:

$$Confidence=\frac{30}{40}=0.75=75\%$$

Lift:

$$Lift=\frac{0.75}{0.50}=1.5$$

Interpretation: 30% of all transactions contain both items. Among transactions containing bread, 75% also contain milk. The lift of 1.5 indicates that bread and milk occur together 1.5 times as frequently as expected under independence.

Additional interestingness measures

  • Leverage: Measures the difference between observed joint support and expected joint support under independence.

$$Leverage(X,Y)=Support(X\cup Y)-Support(X)Support(Y)$$

  • Conviction: Measures the degree to which the occurrence of X is associated with the absence of exceptions to the rule.

$$Conviction(X\Rightarrow Y)=\frac{1-Support(Y)}{1-Confidence(X\Rightarrow Y)}$$

Conviction is conventionally treated as infinite when confidence is 1 and support of Y is below 1.

Important distinction

Support measures frequency, confidence measures conditional occurrence, and lift measures association relative to independence. A rule with high confidence may still have a lift close to 1 when its consequent is already very common.

children.title: 1.3 Frequent Itemset Mining
children.body:
Frequent Itemsets

A frequent itemset is a set of items that appears in a transaction database with support greater than or equal to a user-defined minimum support threshold.

Minimum support

Minimum support is the threshold used to determine whether an itemset is frequent.

$$Minimum\ Support=\text{user-defined support threshold}$$

For example, if the minimum support is 20%, an itemset must occur in at least 20% of all transactions to be considered frequent.

Apriori principle

The Apriori principle states that every non-empty subset of a frequent itemset must also be frequent. Equivalently, if an itemset is infrequent, all of its supersets must also be infrequent.

This property is also called the downward closure or anti-monotonicity property of support.

Example

If the itemset {Bread, Milk, Butter} is frequent, then all its non-empty subsets must also be frequent:

  • {Bread}
  • {Milk}
  • {Butter}
  • {Bread, Milk}
  • {Bread, Butter}
  • {Milk, Butter}

If {Bread, Milk} is infrequent, then {Bread, Milk, Butter} and any other superset containing {Bread, Milk} can be pruned without calculating their support.

Candidate and frequent itemsets

  • Candidate itemset: An itemset generated for support counting.
  • Frequent itemset: A candidate whose support meets the minimum support threshold.
  • Candidate generation: The process of constructing larger itemsets from smaller frequent itemsets.
  • Pruning: Removing candidates that cannot be frequent based on the Apriori principle.

Frequent itemset mining process

  1. Find frequent 1-itemsets.
  2. Use frequent 1-itemsets to generate candidate 2-itemsets.
  3. Prune candidates whose subsets are not frequent.
  4. Count candidate supports by scanning the database.
  5. Retain candidates meeting minimum support.
  6. Repeat for larger itemsets until no new frequent itemsets are found.

children.title: 1.4 Apriori Algorithm
children.body:
Apriori Algorithm

Apriori is a classic frequent itemset mining algorithm used in association rule analysis. It discovers frequent itemsets by generating candidates level by level and pruning candidates using the Apriori property.

Working principle

Apriori first identifies frequent single items, then uses them to generate larger candidate itemsets. Candidates are checked against the minimum support threshold. Itemsets that do not satisfy the threshold are discarded.

Algorithm steps

  1. Scan the transaction database and calculate the support of each individual item.
  2. Remove items that do not satisfy minimum support. The remaining items form frequent 1-itemsets, denoted L1.
  3. Generate candidate 2-itemsets, C2, by joining frequent 1-itemsets.
  4. Prune any candidate whose non-empty proper subsets are not all frequent.
  5. Scan the database and count the support of each remaining candidate.
  6. Retain candidates satisfying minimum support to form L2.
  7. Repeat the join, prune and support-counting process to generate L3, L4 and subsequent levels.
  8. Stop when no new frequent itemsets are generated.

Pseudocode

L1 = frequent 1-itemsets
k = 2

while L(k-1) is not empty:
    Ck = generate candidates from L(k-1)
    prune candidates whose subsets are not frequent

    for each transaction T in database:
        count support of candidates contained in T

    Lk = candidates in Ck meeting minimum support
    k = k + 1

return all frequent itemsets

Numerical example

Consider the following transaction database:

TransactionItems
T1Bread, Milk
T2Bread, Diaper, Beer, Eggs
T3Milk, Diaper, Beer, Cola
T4Bread, Milk, Diaper, Beer
T5Bread, Milk, Diaper, Cola

Let minimum support count = 3 transactions, equivalent to 60%.

Step 1: Find frequent 1-itemsets

ItemSupport countFrequent?
Bread4Yes
Milk4Yes
Diaper4Yes
Beer3Yes
Eggs1No
Cola2No

Therefore, L1 = {Bread}, {Milk}, {Diaper}, {Beer}.

Step 2: Generate and count candidate 2-itemsets

CandidateSupport countFrequent?
Bread, Milk3Yes
Bread, Diaper3Yes
Bread, Beer2No
Milk, Diaper3Yes
Milk, Beer2No
Diaper, Beer3Yes

Thus L2 contains {Bread, Milk}, {Bread, Diaper}, {Milk, Diaper} and {Diaper, Beer}.

Step 3: Generate candidate 3-itemsets

Candidate {Bread, Milk, Diaper} is generated because all its 2-item subsets are frequent. Its support count is 2, from T4 and T5, so it is not frequent.

Other possible 3-itemsets are pruned when one or more of their 2-item subsets are not frequent.

No frequent 3-itemset remains. Therefore, the algorithm stops.

Advantages

  • Simple and easy to understand.
  • Uses the Apriori property to reduce candidate itemsets.
  • Produces frequent itemsets that can be used to generate association rules.

Disadvantages

  • Requires repeated scans of the transaction database.
  • May generate a large number of candidate itemsets.
  • Can require substantial memory for candidate storage and support counting.
  • Can be inefficient for dense datasets or low minimum support thresholds.

children.title: 1.5 Association Rule Generation
children.body:
Generating Association Rules

Once frequent itemsets have been discovered, association rules can be generated from them. A frequent itemset is divided into two non-empty, disjoint subsets to form a rule.

For a frequent itemset F, a rule can be written as:

$$X\Rightarrow(F-X)$$

Where X is a non-empty proper subset of F.

Rule generation steps

  1. Take a frequent itemset F containing at least two items.
  2. Generate all non-empty proper subsets X of F.
  3. For each subset X, create the rule $X\Rightarrow(F-X)$.
  4. Calculate the confidence of each rule.
  5. Retain rules satisfying the minimum confidence threshold.
  6. Calculate lift or other interestingness measures when required.

Example

Suppose {Bread, Milk, Butter} is a frequent itemset. Possible rules include:

  • {Bread, Milk} → {Butter}
  • {Bread, Butter} → {Milk}
  • {Milk, Butter} → {Bread}
  • {Bread} → {Milk, Butter}
  • {Milk} → {Bread, Butter}
  • {Butter} → {Bread, Milk}

Each rule has the same support because its union is the same complete itemset. However, the confidence values can differ because the antecedent supports differ.

Important points

  • Association rules are directional: $X\Rightarrow Y$ and $Y\Rightarrow X$ can have different confidence values.
  • Support is the same for a rule and its reverse because both use the same union of items.
  • Confidence is not symmetric.
  • Rules must have non-empty antecedent and consequent sets.
  • High confidence does not imply causation.

children.title: 1.6 FP-Growth Algorithm
children.body:
FP-Growth

FP-Growth stands for Frequent Pattern Growth. It is a frequent itemset mining algorithm that avoids generating large candidate itemsets. Instead, it compresses the transaction database into a structure called an FP-tree and mines frequent patterns from this structure.

FP-tree

An FP-tree, or Frequent Pattern Tree, is a compact prefix-tree representation of a transaction database. Transactions are represented by paths. Common prefixes are shared, and each node stores an item and its occurrence count.

Important components

  • Root: The starting node of the tree, usually labelled null.
  • Item node: Stores an item and its count.
  • Node links: Connect nodes containing the same item.
  • Header table: Maintains frequent items and links to their corresponding nodes.
  • Conditional pattern base: A collection of prefix paths associated with a particular item.
  • Conditional FP-tree: A smaller FP-tree constructed from a conditional pattern base.

FP-Growth algorithm steps

  1. Scan the transaction database and calculate the support count of every item.
  2. Remove items that do not meet minimum support.
  3. Sort the remaining frequent items in descending order of global support.
  4. Scan the database again and reorder each transaction according to the global frequent-item order.
  5. Insert the ordered transactions into an FP-tree, sharing common prefixes and incrementing node counts.
  6. Construct a header table and node links for the frequent items.
  7. Mine the FP-tree from the least frequent item towards the most frequent item in the header table.
  8. For each item, construct its conditional pattern base.
  9. Build the corresponding conditional FP-tree.
  10. Recursively mine conditional FP-trees to generate frequent patterns.

Small illustrative example

Consider these transactions:

TransactionItems
T1A, B, D
T2B, C, E
T3A, B, C, E
T4B, E

Assume minimum support count = 2.

  1. Count item frequencies: A = 2, B = 4, C = 2, D = 1, E = 3.
  2. Remove D because its support is below 2.
  3. Sort frequent items by descending support: B, E, A, C. Ties may be resolved using a consistent ordering.
  4. Reorder the transactions and insert them into the FP-tree. Common prefixes such as B are shared and their counts are increased.
  5. Use the header table to construct conditional pattern bases and conditional FP-trees.
  6. Recursively mine these trees to discover frequent itemsets.

Advantages

  • Avoids explicit candidate itemset generation.
  • Usually requires only two full scans of the transaction database to construct the FP-tree.
  • Compresses databases with shared transaction prefixes.
  • Can be more efficient than Apriori for many dense datasets.

Disadvantages

  • FP-tree construction and recursive mining can be complex to implement.
  • The tree may consume substantial memory for datasets with few shared prefixes.
  • Conditional pattern bases and conditional trees can become large.
  • Performance depends on the data structure and dataset characteristics.

children.title: 1.7 Apriori versus FP-Growth
children.body:
Comparison of Apriori and FP-Growth

FeatureAprioriFP-Growth
Main approachCandidate generation and testingPattern growth using an FP-tree
Candidate generationGenerates candidate itemsets level by levelAvoids explicit candidate generation
Database scansRequires repeated scans for successive itemset sizesUsually uses two full database scans to build the FP-tree
Data structureCandidate itemset collectionsFP-tree and header table
PruningUses the Apriori propertyUses conditional pattern bases and conditional FP-trees
Memory useCan require substantial memory for candidatesRequires memory for the FP-tree and conditional structures
ImplementationRelatively simpleMore complex
Typical performanceCan be slow when many candidates are generatedOften faster when the FP-tree compresses the data effectively

When to use

  • Apriori: Useful for learning frequent itemset mining, smaller datasets and situations where a straightforward candidate-based method is suitable.
  • FP-Growth: Useful when candidate generation is expensive and the database can be compressed effectively into an FP-tree.

Neither algorithm is universally faster. Performance depends on transaction size, database density, support threshold, memory availability and implementation.

children.title: 2.1 Introduction to Web Mining
children.body:
Web Mining

Web Mining is the application of data mining techniques to discover useful information and patterns from web-related data. It includes analysing web page content, hyperlink structures and user interaction records.

Types of Web Mining

1. Web Content Mining

Web Content Mining extracts useful information from the contents of web pages. The content may include text, images, audio, video, metadata and structured data.

Examples include extracting product information from online stores, collecting news articles and analysing the text of web pages.

2. Web Structure Mining

Web Structure Mining analyses the hyperlink structure of the web. It represents web pages as nodes and hyperlinks as directed edges to identify relationships, authorities and important pages.

Examples include link analysis, identifying authoritative pages and ranking web pages using PageRank.

3. Web Usage Mining

Web Usage Mining analyses user interaction data such as server logs, browser activity, clickstreams and page navigation sequences. It is used to understand browsing behaviour and improve website design.

Applications of web mining

  • Search engine ranking.
  • Personalized recommendations.
  • Customer behaviour analysis.
  • Website optimization.
  • Targeted content delivery.
  • Detection of unusual web activity.

Comparison of web mining types

TypeData analysedExample
Content miningText, images, media and page contentExtracting product details from web pages
Structure miningLinks and relationships between pagesPageRank
Usage miningLogs, clicks and navigation patternsAnalysing user browsing sequences

children.title: 2.2 Web Structure Mining
children.body:
Web Structure Mining

Web Structure Mining studies the link relationships among web pages. A website or the web can be represented as a directed graph in which each web page is a vertex and each hyperlink is a directed edge.

Graph representation

  • Vertex: Represents a web page.
  • Directed edge: Represents a hyperlink from one page to another.
  • In-link: A link pointing to a page from another page.
  • Out-link: A link from a page to another page.

Importance of link analysis

  • Identifies important and authoritative pages.
  • Helps search engines rank web pages.
  • Discovers relationships among websites.
  • Supports analysis of web communities and link networks.

Example

If page A links to page B, the graph contains a directed edge A → B. If many important pages link to B, B may be considered an important page. PageRank formalizes this idea by considering both the number and importance of incoming links.

children.title: 2.3 PageRank Algorithm
children.body:
PageRank

PageRank is a link analysis algorithm originally developed for ranking web pages. It estimates the importance of a page based on the links pointing to it and the importance of the pages providing those links.

The central idea is that a link from an important page contributes more to the importance of the linked page than a link from a less important page.

Random surfer model

PageRank can be understood using the random surfer model. A hypothetical user follows links from the current page with a certain probability and occasionally jumps to another page at random. The PageRank value represents the long-run probability of the surfer being on a particular page under the model.

PageRank formula

$$PR(A)=\frac{1-d}{N}+d\sum_{T_i\in In(A)}\frac{PR(T_i)}{C(T_i)}$$

Where:

  • $PR(A)$ is the PageRank of page A.
  • d is the damping factor, commonly set to 0.85 in the traditional formulation.
  • N is the total number of pages in the graph.
  • $In(A)$ is the set of pages linking to A.
  • $PR(T_i)$ is the PageRank of a page linking to A.
  • $C(T_i)$ is the number of outgoing links from page $T_i$.

Interpretation

  • The term $(1-d)/N$ represents the random-jump contribution in the simplified formula for pages without dangling-link complications.
  • The summation distributes the PageRank of linking pages among their outgoing links.
  • The damping factor controls the contribution from following links versus random jumps.

Numerical example

Suppose a web graph contains 3 pages: A, B and C. Assume:

  • A links to B and C.
  • B links to C.
  • C links to A.

Let d = 0.85 and initialize all page ranks to 1/3.

Page A receives a link from C:

$$PR(A)=\frac{0.15}{3}+0.85\times\frac{1}{3}\approx0.3333$$

Page B receives a link from A, which has two outgoing links:

$$PR(B)=\frac{0.15}{3}+0.85\times\frac{1/3}{2}\approx0.1917$$

Page C receives links from A and B:

$$PR(C)=\frac{0.15}{3}+0.85\left(\frac{1/3}{2}+\frac{1/3}{1}\right)\approx0.4750$$

These are the results of one update iteration, not the final converged PageRank values. The process is repeated until the ranks converge sufficiently.

PageRank algorithm steps

  1. Represent web pages as nodes and hyperlinks as directed edges.
  2. Initialize PageRank values, commonly to 1/N for each page.
  3. Calculate each page's new rank using the ranks of its incoming-link pages.
  4. Apply the damping factor and account for random jumps.
  5. Handle pages with no outgoing links by distributing their rank appropriately across the graph.
  6. Repeat the calculation until the rank values change by less than a specified tolerance or a maximum number of iterations is reached.

Dangling pages

A dangling page is a page with no outgoing links. If its rank is not redistributed, rank mass can disappear during iteration. A standard PageRank formulation treats a dangling page as linking uniformly to all pages, or equivalently redistributes its rank across the graph.

Advantages

  • Uses the link structure of the web to estimate page importance.
  • Considers the importance of linking pages, not only the number of incoming links.
  • Can be computed iteratively using matrix operations.

Limitations

  • PageRank alone does not measure how relevant a page is to a particular search query.
  • Link structures can be manipulated through link spam.
  • Results depend on graph structure and model assumptions.
  • Modern search engines use many additional ranking signals and systems; PageRank is not a complete description of modern search ranking.

children.title: 2.4 HITS Algorithm: Hubs and Authorities
children.body:
HITS Algorithm

HITS stands for Hyperlink-Induced Topic Search. It is a link analysis algorithm that assigns two scores to web pages: an authority score and a hub score.

Authority

An authority is a page that contains valuable information about a topic. A page receives a high authority score when many good hub pages link to it.

Hub

A hub is a page that links to several useful authority pages. A page receives a high hub score when it links to pages with high authority scores.

HITS scoring principle

  • A page's authority score is the sum of the hub scores of pages linking to it.
  • A page's hub score is the sum of the authority scores of pages it links to.

For a page p:

$$Authority(p)=\sum_{q\rightarrow p}Hub(q)$$

$$Hub(p)=\sum_{p\rightarrow r}Authority(r)$$

Algorithm steps

  1. Construct a focused subgraph of pages relevant to a query or topic.
  2. Initialize hub and authority scores.
  3. Update authority scores using the hub scores of incoming-link pages.
  4. Update hub scores using the authority scores of outgoing-link pages.
  5. Normalize the scores.
  6. Repeat until the scores stabilize.

PageRank versus HITS

PageRankHITS
Assigns one main importance score to each page.Assigns separate hub and authority scores.
Uses a random-surfer interpretation.Uses mutual reinforcement between hubs and authorities.
Traditionally computed over a broad web graph.Traditionally computed on a query-focused subgraph.
Uses a damping factor in its standard formulation.Uses iterative score updates and normalization.

children.title: 3.1 Introduction to Web Usage Mining
children.body:
Web Usage Mining

Web Usage Mining is the process of discovering user access patterns and browsing behaviour from web usage data. It analyses records generated when users interact with websites and web applications.

Objectives

  • Understand user navigation behaviour.
  • Identify frequently visited pages.
  • Discover common browsing sequences.
  • Improve website structure and usability.
  • Personalize content and recommendations.
  • Support website performance analysis.

Sources of web usage data

  • Web server logs: Record requests received by a web server.
  • Proxy server logs: Record requests passing through a proxy server.
  • Browser logs: Record browsing activity on a client device where available.
  • Application logs: Record user actions within a web application.
  • Clickstream data: Records the sequence of pages or elements clicked by a user.
  • Cookies and session identifiers: May help distinguish visits or maintain session state, subject to privacy and consent requirements.

Example

A website may discover that users who visit a product page frequently visit its review page next. This pattern can be used to improve page navigation or recommend related content.

Applications

  • E-commerce personalization.
  • Website redesign and navigation optimization.
  • Recommendation systems.
  • Customer behaviour analysis.
  • Detection of unusual access patterns.
  • Content management and targeted advertising.

children.title: 3.2 Web Server Logs
children.body:
Web Server Log Data

Web server logs are files that record requests made to a web server. They are an important source of data for web usage mining.

Common log fields

  • IP address: Address associated with the requesting client or network.
  • Timestamp: Date and time of the request.
  • Request method: HTTP method such as GET or POST.
  • Requested resource: URL or resource requested by the client.
  • Status code: HTTP response status, such as 200, 404 or 500.
  • Bytes transferred: Size of the response.
  • Referrer: The referring page, when supplied.
  • User agent: Browser or client software information supplied with the request.

Example log entry

192.0.2.10 - - [05/Nov/2026:10:30:00 +0530] "GET /products/item1 HTTP/1.1" 200 2048 "https://example.com/" "Mozilla/5.0"

This example represents a GET request for /products/item1, which received HTTP status 200 and transferred 2048 bytes. The IP address and other fields are illustrative.

Challenges in log analysis

  • One user may access a site from multiple devices or IP addresses.
  • Multiple users may share one public IP address.
  • Browser and proxy caching can hide requests from server logs.
  • Automated bots can generate large volumes of traffic.
  • Missing referrer information can make navigation reconstruction difficult.
  • Privacy requirements restrict the collection and processing of identifiable browsing data.

children.title: 3.3 Web Usage Mining Process
children.body:
Stages of Web Usage Mining

Web usage mining generally involves data collection, preprocessing, pattern discovery and pattern analysis.

1. Data collection

Collect data from web server logs, application logs, proxy logs, clickstreams and other permitted sources.

2. Data preprocessing

Convert raw log data into a structured form suitable for analysis.

  • Data cleaning: Remove irrelevant requests, errors and unwanted records. For example, requests for images, stylesheets and scripts may be excluded when analysing page navigation.
  • User identification: Distinguish users using available identifiers and suitable heuristics. IP address and user agent combinations may be used, but they do not guarantee accurate identification.
  • Session identification: Divide user activity into individual visits or sessions.
  • Path completion: Infer missing page requests where possible, taking browser caching and other factors into account.
  • Formatting: Convert timestamps, URLs and other fields into consistent representations.

3. Pattern discovery

Apply data mining algorithms to discover patterns in the preprocessed data.

  • Association rule mining.
  • Sequential pattern mining.
  • Clustering.
  • Classification.
  • Statistical analysis.

4. Pattern analysis

Interpret the discovered patterns, remove uninteresting results and use meaningful findings for website improvement or business decisions.

Overall process

$$Data\ Collection\rightarrow Preprocessing\rightarrow Pattern\ Discovery\rightarrow Pattern\ Analysis$$

children.title: 3.4 User Identification and Session Identification
children.body:
User Identification

User identification is the process of determining which requests belong to the same user. This is necessary because raw web logs record individual requests rather than complete user journeys.

Common techniques

  • Authentication: Uses a logged-in account identifier when available and appropriate.
  • Cookies: Uses a browser identifier to associate requests with a browser over time.
  • IP address and user agent: Uses network address and client information as a heuristic when stronger identifiers are unavailable.

These techniques have limitations. Shared devices, dynamic IP addresses, privacy controls and multiple devices can make user identification uncertain.

Session Identification

Session identification, also called sessionization, divides a user's sequence of requests into separate visits or sessions.

Common approaches

  • Timeout-based method: Starts a new session when the time between consecutive requests exceeds a chosen inactivity threshold, commonly 30 minutes in simple examples.
  • Cookie-based method: Uses session identifiers supplied by the website.
  • Login-based method: Uses explicit login or logout events to define session boundaries when available.
  • Navigation-based method: Uses page relationships and browsing paths to help identify session boundaries.

Example

Suppose a user accesses pages at 10:00, 10:05, 10:12 and 11:00. With a 30-minute inactivity threshold, the first three requests belong to one session and the 11:00 request begins a new session.

Importance

  • Helps reconstruct user browsing journeys.
  • Supports page sequence and association analysis.
  • Allows calculation of session duration and page views per session.
  • Improves website personalization and usability analysis.

children.title: 3.5 Pattern Discovery in Web Usage Mining
children.body:
Pattern Discovery Techniques

1. Association rule mining

Finds pages or actions that frequently occur together within user sessions. Example: users who visit a product details page often visit its reviews page.

2. Sequential pattern mining

Discovers frequent ordered sequences of user actions or page visits. Example: Home → Category → Product → Checkout. Unlike ordinary association rules, sequential patterns preserve the order of events.

3. Clustering

Groups users or web pages based on similar behaviour or characteristics. For example, visitors may be grouped into frequent buyers, occasional visitors and information seekers.

4. Classification

Predicts a predefined category using labelled historical data. For example, predicting whether a visitor is likely to complete a purchase.

5. Statistical analysis

Uses descriptive measures such as page views, visit duration, bounce rate and frequency of visits to summarize web usage.

Uses of discovered patterns

  • Recommend relevant pages and products.
  • Identify confusing website navigation paths.
  • Improve page layout and content placement.
  • Understand conversion paths and drop-off points.
  • Identify unusual traffic patterns.

children.title: 4.1 Introduction to Text Mining
children.body:
Text Mining

Text Mining is the process of extracting useful information, patterns and knowledge from unstructured or semi-structured textual data. It combines techniques from data mining, natural language processing, information retrieval and machine learning.

Sources of text data

  • News articles and web pages.
  • Customer reviews and feedback.
  • Emails and support messages.
  • Research papers and reports.
  • Social media posts.
  • Product descriptions and online discussions.

Characteristics of text data

  • Usually unstructured or semi-structured.
  • Contains words, phrases, sentences and documents.
  • Can contain spelling errors, abbreviations and ambiguous expressions.
  • May contain irrelevant words and repeated information.
  • Often requires preprocessing before analysis.

Applications

  • Sentiment analysis.
  • Spam detection.
  • Document classification.
  • Topic identification.
  • News categorization.
  • Information extraction.
  • Customer feedback analysis.

Text mining process

  1. Collect documents from relevant sources.
  2. Clean and normalize the text.
  3. Tokenize the text into words or other units.
  4. Remove irrelevant terms where appropriate.
  5. Apply stemming or lemmatization if required.
  6. Convert text into numerical representations.
  7. Apply data mining or machine learning techniques.
  8. Interpret and evaluate the results.

children.title: 4.2 Text Preprocessing
children.body:
Text Preprocessing

Text preprocessing converts raw text into a cleaner and more consistent representation for analysis. It reduces noise and helps algorithms process documents effectively.

1. Tokenization

Tokenization divides text into smaller units called tokens. Tokens may be words, sentences, characters or subword units.

Example:

Original text: Data mining discovers useful patterns.

Word tokens: [Data, mining, discovers, useful, patterns]

2. Case folding

Converts text into a consistent letter case, usually lowercase.

Example: Data Mining → data mining.

3. Stop-word removal

Removes frequently occurring words that may contribute little to a particular analysis, such as 'the', 'is', 'and' and 'of'. Stop-word removal must be task-dependent because some common words can carry important meaning.

4. Stemming

Stemming reduces words to a common stem by removing prefixes or suffixes using heuristic rules.

Example: connected, connecting and connection may be reduced to a common stem such as connect, depending on the stemmer.

5. Lemmatization

Lemmatization converts words to their dictionary base form, called a lemma, using linguistic information.

Example: better → good in a context-aware lemmatization system; running → run.

Stemming versus lemmatization

StemmingLemmatization
Uses rule-based removal of word endings.Uses vocabulary and linguistic analysis.
May produce non-dictionary stems.Produces valid dictionary base forms in supported cases.
Usually faster and simpler.Usually more computationally demanding.
Does not always consider grammatical context.Can use part-of-speech and context information.

6. Removing noise

Depending on the task, preprocessing may remove HTML tags, URLs, punctuation, duplicated text, malformed characters and irrelevant symbols.

7. Part-of-speech tagging

Assigns grammatical categories such as noun, verb, adjective and adverb to tokens. It can support lemmatization and more advanced language analysis.

8. Named Entity Recognition

Identifies named entities such as people, organizations, locations, dates and monetary values in text.

children.title: 4.3 Text Representation and Feature Extraction
children.body:
Representing Text Numerically

Most machine learning algorithms require numerical input. Text documents must therefore be transformed into numerical feature vectors.

1. Bag of Words

The Bag of Words (BoW) model represents a document using the frequency of words in a vocabulary. It ignores word order and focuses on word occurrence or counts.

Example documents:

  • D1: data mining is useful
  • D2: data science is useful

Vocabulary: [data, mining, is, useful, science].

Documentdataminingisusefulscience
D111110
D210111

2. Term Frequency

Term Frequency (TF) measures how frequently a term appears in a document.

One common normalized definition is:

$$TF(t,d)=\frac{f_{t,d}}{\sum_{t'}f_{t',d}}$$

Where $f_{t,d}$ is the frequency of term t in document d. Other TF conventions, such as raw counts or logarithmic scaling, are also used.

3. Inverse Document Frequency

Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) measures how informative a term is across a collection of documents. Terms appearing in many documents receive lower IDF values.

A common definition is:

$$IDF(t)=\log\frac{N}{df(t)}$$

Where N is the total number of documents and $df(t)$ is the number of documents containing term t.

4. TF-IDF

TF-IDF combines term frequency and inverse document frequency to assign a weight to each term in a document.

$$TFIDF(t,d)=TF(t,d)\times IDF(t)$$

A term receives a high weight when it occurs frequently in a particular document but appears in relatively few documents across the collection.

TF-IDF example

Suppose there are 100 documents. The term 'mining' occurs in 10 documents. Using the basic IDF formula:

$$IDF(mining)=\log_{10}\left(\frac{100}{10}\right)=1$$

If its normalized term frequency in a document is 0.2, then:

$$TFIDF=0.2\times1=0.2$$

This is an illustrative calculation using base-10 logarithms and normalized TF.

5. N-grams

An n-gram is a sequence of n consecutive tokens. Unigrams contain one token, bigrams contain two consecutive tokens and trigrams contain three consecutive tokens.

Example: 'data mining techniques'.

  • Unigrams: data, mining, techniques.
  • Bigrams: data mining, mining techniques.
  • Trigram: data mining techniques.

N-grams preserve some local word-order information that a basic Bag of Words model ignores.

6. Word embeddings

Word embeddings represent words as dense numerical vectors. Words used in similar contexts may have similar vector representations. Unlike basic Bag of Words features, embeddings can capture aspects of semantic similarity.

Limitations of basic Bag of Words and TF-IDF

  • They do not fully capture word order or sentence structure.
  • They can produce large and sparse feature vectors.
  • They may not capture synonyms or contextual meaning effectively.
  • TF-IDF weights depend on the document collection and preprocessing choices.

children.title: 4.4 Text Classification
children.body:
Text Classification

Text classification assigns predefined categories to text documents. It is a supervised learning task when labelled examples are available.

Examples

  • Classifying emails as spam or not spam.
  • Classifying news articles as sports, politics or technology.
  • Classifying customer reviews as positive, negative or neutral.
  • Classifying support requests by issue category.

Text classification process

  1. Collect a set of labelled documents.
  2. Clean and preprocess the text.
  3. Convert documents into numerical features using methods such as Bag of Words or TF-IDF.
  4. Divide the data into training, validation and test sets.
  5. Train a classifier using the training data.
  6. Evaluate the model using appropriate classification metrics.
  7. Use the trained classifier to assign labels to new documents.

Common algorithms

  • Naive Bayes: A probabilistic classifier based on Bayes' theorem and a conditional independence assumption between features given the class.
  • Support Vector Machine: Finds a decision boundary that separates classes, often using TF-IDF features for text classification.
  • Decision Tree: Learns a set of feature-based decision rules.
  • Logistic Regression: Estimates class probabilities using a linear combination of input features.
  • Neural Networks: Learn complex relationships from numerical text representations.

Evaluation

Text classifiers can be evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-Score and confusion matrices. For imbalanced text datasets, precision, recall and F1-Score are often more informative than accuracy alone.

children.title: 4.5 Sentiment Analysis
children.body:
Sentiment Analysis

Sentiment Analysis is a text mining technique used to identify opinions, emotions or attitudes expressed in text. It is commonly used to determine whether a review or comment expresses positive, negative or neutral sentiment.

Types of sentiment analysis

  • Document-level: Assigns an overall sentiment to an entire document.
  • Sentence-level: Identifies the sentiment expressed in an individual sentence.
  • Aspect-based: Identifies sentiment towards specific aspects of a product or service.
  • Fine-grained: Uses more detailed categories, such as very positive, positive, neutral, negative and very negative.

Approaches

1. Lexicon-based approach

Uses a sentiment dictionary containing words associated with positive or negative polarity. A document's sentiment is estimated from the sentiment values of its words.

2. Machine learning approach

Trains a classifier on labelled text examples. Features may include word counts, TF-IDF vectors, n-grams or embeddings.

3. Deep learning approach

Uses neural network models to learn representations and sentiment patterns. Depending on the architecture, these models may capture contextual information and relationships between words.

Example

  • Review: 'The camera quality is excellent.' Sentiment: Positive.
  • Review: 'The battery life is disappointing.' Sentiment: Negative.
  • Review: 'The package arrived yesterday.' Sentiment: Neutral, depending on context.

Challenges

  • Negation: 'Not good' expresses a different meaning from 'good'.
  • Sarcasm: Literal words may express the opposite of the intended sentiment.
  • Context: A word may be positive in one domain and negative in another.
  • Mixed sentiment: A review may praise one feature and criticize another.
  • Slang and spelling variations: Informal language can make interpretation difficult.
  • Multilingual text: Different languages and code-mixed text require suitable language processing.

Applications

  • Product review analysis.
  • Brand and reputation monitoring.
  • Customer feedback analysis.
  • Social media opinion analysis.
  • Service quality assessment.

children.title: 4.6 Information Retrieval
children.body:
Information Retrieval

Information Retrieval (IR) is the process of finding relevant documents or information from a large collection in response to a user's query. Search engines, digital libraries and document search systems are common examples.

Information Retrieval system

An information retrieval system typically contains the following components:

  • Document collection: The set of documents that can be searched.
  • Document preprocessing: Processes text through tokenization, normalization and other operations.
  • Indexing: Creates a data structure that supports efficient searching.
  • Query processing: Converts a user's query into a searchable representation.
  • Matching and ranking: Finds documents matching the query and orders them by estimated relevance.
  • Result presentation: Displays ranked results to the user.

Basic information retrieval process

  1. Collect and preprocess documents.
  2. Build an index of document terms.
  3. Accept a user query.
  4. Preprocess the query in a manner compatible with document processing.
  5. Retrieve documents matching the query.
  6. Rank the retrieved documents by relevance.
  7. Display the results.

Inverted index

An inverted index is a data structure that maps each term to the list of documents containing that term. It allows a search engine to locate documents efficiently without scanning every document for every query.

Example:

TermPosting list
dataD1, D2, D3
miningD1, D3
retrievalD2

For the query 'data mining', the system can retrieve documents associated with both terms and rank them using its retrieval model.

Boolean retrieval

Boolean retrieval uses logical operators to match documents against a query.

  • AND: Retrieves documents containing both terms.
  • OR: Retrieves documents containing either term or both.
  • NOT: Excludes documents containing a specified term.

Example: 'data AND mining' retrieves documents containing both data and mining.

Ranking-based retrieval

Ranking-based retrieval assigns relevance scores to documents and sorts results by score. TF-IDF and BM25 are examples of term-based ranking approaches. Modern search systems may use additional semantic and machine-learning-based ranking methods.

children.title: 4.7 Precision and Recall in Information Retrieval
children.body:
Information Retrieval Evaluation

Precision and recall are commonly used to evaluate the quality of retrieved search results.

Precision

Precision measures the proportion of retrieved documents that are relevant.

$$Precision=\frac{\text{Relevant documents retrieved}}{\text{Total documents retrieved}}$$

Recall

Recall measures the proportion of all relevant documents that are retrieved.

$$Recall=\frac{\text{Relevant documents retrieved}}{\text{Total relevant documents in collection}}$$

F1-Score

The F1-Score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

$$F1=2\times\frac{Precision\times Recall}{Precision+Recall}$$

Numerical example

Suppose a search system retrieves 20 documents. Of these, 15 are relevant. The complete collection contains 30 relevant documents.

Precision:

$$Precision=\frac{15}{20}=0.75=75\%$$

Recall:

$$Recall=\frac{15}{30}=0.50=50\%$$

F1-Score:

$$F1=2\times\frac{0.75\times0.50}{0.75+0.50}=0.60=60\%$$

Precision-recall trade-off

  • High precision means fewer irrelevant documents among retrieved results.
  • High recall means a larger proportion of all relevant documents are retrieved.
  • Increasing the number of retrieved documents may improve recall but can reduce precision.
  • The appropriate balance depends on the search application.

Other retrieval evaluation measures

  • Mean Average Precision (MAP): Averages average precision across multiple queries and considers the ranking of relevant documents.
  • Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR): Measures the reciprocal rank of the first relevant result and averages it across queries.
  • Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG): Evaluates ranked results using graded relevance and gives higher importance to relevant documents appearing near the top.

children.title: 4.8 Text Mining versus Information Retrieval
children.body:
Text Mining and Information Retrieval

Text MiningInformation Retrieval
Discovers patterns, trends and knowledge from text.Finds documents relevant to a user's information need.
Focuses on analysis and knowledge extraction.Focuses on searching, matching and ranking.
May use classification, clustering and sentiment analysis.May use indexing, Boolean matching and ranking models.
Example: identifying customer sentiment from reviews.Example: retrieving relevant research papers for a query.

Relationship

Text mining and information retrieval are related fields. Information retrieval can identify relevant documents, while text mining can analyse those documents to discover useful patterns, topics and relationships.

children.title: 5.1 Important Formula Sheet
children.body:
Association Rule Mining

Support:

$$Support(X)=\frac{Count(X)}{N}$$

Rule support:

$$Support(X\Rightarrow Y)=Support(X\cup Y)$$

Confidence:

$$Confidence(X\Rightarrow Y)=\frac{Support(X\cup Y)}{Support(X)}$$

Lift:

$$Lift(X\Rightarrow Y)=\frac{Support(X\cup Y)}{Support(X)Support(Y)}$$

Leverage:

$$Leverage(X,Y)=Support(X\cup Y)-Support(X)Support(Y)$$

Conviction:

$$Conviction(X\Rightarrow Y)=\frac{1-Support(Y)}{1-Confidence(X\Rightarrow Y)}$$

PageRank

Basic PageRank equation:

$$PR(A)=\frac{1-d}{N}+d\sum_{T_i\in In(A)}\frac{PR(T_i)}{C(T_i)}$$

For the basic equation, dangling pages require an additional rank redistribution treatment.

Text Mining

Term Frequency:

$$TF(t,d)=\frac{f_{t,d}}{\sum_{t'}f_{t',d}}$$

Inverse Document Frequency:

$$IDF(t)=\log\frac{N}{df(t)}$$

TF-IDF:

$$TFIDF(t,d)=TF(t,d)\times IDF(t)$$

Information Retrieval

Precision:

$$Precision=\frac{Relevant\ retrieved}{Total\ retrieved}$$

Recall:

$$Recall=\frac{Relevant\ retrieved}{Total\ relevant}$$

F1-Score:

$$F1=2\times\frac{Precision\times Recall}{Precision+Recall}$$

Association Rule Mining

  • Define association rule mining and explain its applications.

  • Explain the Apriori principle with an example.
  • Describe the Apriori algorithm with steps and pseudocode.
  • Solve frequent itemset generation problems using candidate generation and pruning.
  • Explain how association rules are generated from frequent itemsets.
  • Explain the FP-tree structure and FP-Growth algorithm.
  • Compare Apriori and FP-Growth.

Web Mining and PageRank

  • Define web mining and explain its three major types.
  • Differentiate web content mining, web structure mining and web usage mining.
  • Explain web structure mining using a directed graph.
  • Explain PageRank and its random surfer model.
  • Write the PageRank equation and explain every term.
  • Solve PageRank numerical problems using iterative updates.
  • Explain dangling pages and the damping factor.
  • Compare PageRank and HITS.

Web Usage Mining

  • Define web usage mining and discuss its applications.
  • Explain the sources and fields of web server log data.
  • Describe the stages of web usage mining.
  • Explain data cleaning, user identification, session identification and path completion.
  • Differentiate user identification and session identification.
  • Explain association, sequential pattern, clustering and classification techniques in web usage mining.

Text Mining and Information Retrieval

  • Define text mining and explain its applications.
  • Explain tokenization, case folding, stop-word removal, stemming and lemmatization.
  • Differentiate stemming and lemmatization.
  • Explain Bag of Words, TF, IDF and TF-IDF with numerical examples.
  • Explain n-grams and word embeddings.
  • Describe the text classification process and common algorithms.
  • Explain sentiment analysis, its approaches and challenges.
  • Define information retrieval and explain the architecture of an IR system.
  • Explain inverted indexing and Boolean retrieval.
  • Calculate precision, recall and F1-Score for retrieved documents.
  • Differentiate text mining and information retrieval.

Numerical problem preparation

  • For association rules, show transaction counts, support, confidence and lift separately.
  • For Apriori, show frequent 1-itemsets, candidate 2-itemsets, pruning, frequent 2-itemsets and subsequent levels.
  • For PageRank, identify incoming links and outgoing-link counts before substituting values into the formula. Show each iteration clearly.
  • For TF-IDF, calculate term frequency, document frequency, inverse document frequency and final weight separately.
  • For information retrieval, identify relevant retrieved documents, total retrieved documents and total relevant documents before calculating precision and recall.

Concepts to remember

  • Apriori uses candidate generation and the downward closure property.
  • FP-Growth uses an FP-tree and conditional pattern bases.
  • Support measures frequency, confidence measures conditional occurrence and lift compares observed association with independence.
  • PageRank measures link-based page importance, not complete query relevance.
  • Web usage mining focuses on user interaction and navigation data.
  • Text mining extracts patterns and knowledge from textual data.
  • Information retrieval finds and ranks documents relevant to a query.
  • Precision measures retrieval correctness, while recall measures retrieval completeness.
